Operations Midnight Hammer and Epic Fury — or at least the lessons learned — were the topics of discussion at a long-range airpower panel during the Air and Space Forces Association’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Sept. 15.
The panel brought together bomber, mobility, and aerospace industry leaders to assess the strategic airpower environment.
Throughout the dialogue, panel members emphasized that while long-range strike operations have proven decisively effective in recent combat campaigns, maintaining that asymmetric advantage demands continuous modernization, seamless cross-command teamwork, and a strong partnership with the defense industrial base.
Maj. Gen. Ty Neuman, Eighth Air Force and Joint-Global Strike Operations Center commander, began by highlighting the inherent stamina of the nation's bomber fleet.
“We are a ready force that demonstrated our endurance,” Neuman said, emphasizing how Eighth Air Force’s constant readiness provides tailored deterrence and reassurance across the globe.
Reflecting on the sheer logistical and operational coordination demanded during Operation Epic Fury, Neuman praised the joint commitment across the enterprise, noting that “everyone has been all in.” He stressed that the unmatched long-range strike capability demonstrated in both Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury delivers an unmistakable message to adversaries: no one should question the readiness or capability of the United States to hold targets at risk anytime, anywhere.
Panelists later discussed the necessity of denying adversaries safe havens and operational sanctuaries, where Neuman outlined why standoff weapons alone cannot shoulder the strategic burden. Potential adversaries continue to harden facilities, bury critical infrastructure, and construct heavily defended anti-access perimeters.
“Not every target can be hit by long-range standoff weapons; we need a penetrating force,” the Eighth Air Force commander said. “Modernizing the legacy bomber fleet is an imperative to denying sanctuary to our adversaries.”
To outpace emerging threats, the Air Force is advancing a complementary mix of weapons and platforms, including standoff systems and stand-in penetrating capabilities. Ongoing modernization efforts include expanding the B-1’s beyond-line-of-sight communication systems, outfitting the B-2 Spirit with advanced radar enhancement programs to bolster survivability in anti-access environments, and exploring expanded payloads for the B-2 fleet.
When operating against advanced air defense systems, stealth remains paramount. “All-aspect low observable weapon systems are a non-negotiable price to entry,” Neuman underscored.
The conversation then moved to the future viability of stealth in an era of proliferating air defense systems.
Neuman affirmed that low observability is not a passing technological phase, but a foundational requirement for the future fight.
He emphasized that the Air Force must pursue both low-observable aircraft and low-observable complementary munitions to survive and deliver effects inside contested airspace. Echoing this assessment, the panel moderator noted that stealth is fundamentally about disrupting the enemy’s integrated kill chain, denying adversaries the ability to detect, track, and engage U.S. strike platforms before mission completion.
The evolving nature of the battlespace, where multi-domain environments are saturated with unmanned systems, electromagnetic interference, and missile salvos, was another topic of discussion.
Industry panelist Jamie Burgess of Boeing cautioned that sheer data volume does not automatically equate to combat capability.
“One can drown in data and starve for information,” Burgess remarked, pointing out the necessity of delivering processed, actionable intelligence directly to aircrews and operational commanders.
The panel discussed how the battle network and integrated command, control, and communications architectures must synthesize real-time data from space, cyber, and airborne assets into coherent situational awareness that accelerates combat decision-making.
Diving into fleet viability and continuous modernization, the general highlighted the operational strain and lessons realized from long-duration strike missions. During Operation Epic Fury, bomber sorties averaged 38 hours in duration — demanding extraordinary human stamina, aircraft reliability, and extensive air refueling support.
According to the Air Mobility Command panelist, “it took dozens and dozens of tankers to execute Operation Epic Fury,” illustrating the indispensable synergy between Air Force Global Strike Command and AMC.
When looking at the service’s age of the inventory, Neuman noted that “our youngest bomber is 30-plus years old.” While airframes have proven durable, sustained investment in modern digital avionics, resilient beyond-line-of-sight connectivity, and modern propulsion is essential across every platform.
The bomber force commander called for a fundamental pivot in weapons integration philosophy: rather than undertaking costly and complex modifications to alter legacy aircraft around new weapons, future munitions must be intentionally designed to seamlessly integrate into existing bomber bays and pylons.
“Bombers must deliver strategic options to the president,” Neuman emphasized, noting that modernization ensures the commander in chief retains flexible, credible conventional and nuclear response options.
Examining the role of industry innovation, Neuman praised the ingenuity of maintenance and logistics Airmen who keep vintage platforms flight-ready, but stressed that the service cannot accomplish sustainment alone.
“It is about partnerships, clear and concise requirements, and giving industry the ability to run with it. It’s a team effort,” Neuman remarked, underscoring the urgent requirement to bolster the defense industrial base and maintain reliable supply chains for critical components.
The panel then concluded by addressing Total Force Integration.
“This is a Total Force Integration effort for every single component,” Neuman said.
“Allies and partners, we have your back. We are the free world’s only long-range strike capability, and we will continue to deliver anytime, anywhere.”
title: Long-range penetrating force remains at forefront of bomber operations

text:
Donohue joined Maj. Gen. Ty W. Neuman, commander of Eighth Air Force and the Joint-Global Strike Operations Center, and Jamie Burgess, vice president and general manager of Mobility, Surveillance and Bombers at Boeing, for a panel discussing long-range airpower with a focus on Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury.
During the discussion, Donohue highlighted the essential role of tanker and strategic airlift platforms in bridging global distances to generate decisive combat power without requiring forward-prepositioned strike forces, emphasizing the historic performance of mobility Airmen who did not miss a single Air Refueling Control Time during recent high-tempo operations.
“When we think about the way we've been able to project power, whether it be from the continental United States or from other locations where it's forward-postured, Air Mobility Command, the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve Command — who are undergoing the biggest mobilization in a generation or two — have been committed all in and extraordinarily effective,” Donohue said. “A tanker fleet that is largely defined by 70-year-old aircraft, sustained by extraordinary maintainers and supported by a global enroute structure to ensure it is ready to meet the challenge, has delivered.”
Echoing the strategic synergy required for global strike, Neuman emphasized that bombers and tankers operate as an inseparable system of systems when executing deep-penetration strikes.
“In the near term, we have to have a combat bomber force that has the long-range strike capability, supported by our AMC brethren, to get to the fight with the appropriate capabilities to inflict the necessary pain and suffering on the adversary,” Neuman said.
“Largely today, some of our forces still operate the way they did 20 years ago, and they don’t have the connectivity that you have when you get on your flights to head home,” Donohue explained. “Epic Fury and Midnight Hammer underscored the importance that connectivity plays — not only to our own survivability, but more importantly, to the success of the Joint Force.”
To illustrate the scale of joint warfighting interoperability, Donohue highlighted the massive refueling and airlift footprint required to launch and recover global strike packages.
“When we talk about Midnight Hammer, most public attention rightly focuses on the extraordinary stealth bomber aircrews who executed the mission. What most Americans don’t fully understand is the dozens and dozens of tankers and airlift assets that were necessary to make that happen,” Donohue stated.
Looking ahead, Donohue cautioned that while the acquisition of the KC-46A Pegasus continues to deliver critical capability, the Air Force must remain clear-eyed about the timelines required to modernize the mobility enterprise.
“The last KC-135 pilot has not been born,” Donohue said. “That is just a statement of fact when we consider the time it takes to modernize and so we will have to sustain our legacy platform as well as our newest platforms and ensure that the Joint Force is supported by being able to execute the mission.”
Donohue concluded by expressing his deep gratitude for the Airmen across active, Guard and Reserve components who make global reach a reality every day.
“The nation should be proud of its mobility Airmen,” Donohue concluded. “Whether it’s in our global AOC, the 618th Air Operations Center, our contingency response, or our global air mobility support structure…we have set the theater. And then ultimately, to the tanker aircrews who made every one of the [Air Refueling Control Times] to ensure that [Neuman’s] team can deliver the desired effects, we should all be proud of what that force is able to accomplish.”
title: AMC deputy commander emphasizes long-range airpower, mobility integration at AFA 2026

ST. LOUIS – A convicted felon from Berkeley, Missouri on Tuesday admitted being caught with two guns in a stolen car after a shootout and police chase last year.

Ja’Lon Pittman, 22, of Berkeley, pleaded guilty in U.S. District Court in St. Louis to one count of being a felon in possession of a firearm. He admitted being caught with a stolen AK-style pistol and a Glock pistol on July 28, 2025. Earlier that day, a man told the Columbia, Missouri police that Pittman had taken his Chrysler 300 without his permission, and possibly his watch and gun. The victim told officers that he located Pittman and during a confrontation, the two exchanged gunfire. Police notified the Missouri State Highway Patrol that Pittman may be heading to the St. Louis area, and troopers spotted him and tried to stop him on Interstate 70. Pittman sped away, driving in excess of 120 m.p.h. and weaving in and out of traffic before crashing near the Blanchette Bridge. Pittman ran away but was found hiding under a van in a nearby parking lot. Investigators found the victim’s Romarm Cugir Micro Draco pistol in the car and a Glock in a bag that Pittman discarded. Pittman was wearing the stolen watch.

The Columbia Police Department, the Missouri State Highway Patrol and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Jennifer Szczucinski prosecuted the case.

This case is part of Project Safe Neighborhoods (PSN), the Department of Justice’s nationwide initiative that brings federal, state, local, and tribal law enforcement, prosecutors, and other public safety partners together to coordinate efforts to combat violent crime and make communities safe. Coordinated by U.S. Attorneys’ offices in each of the 94 federal districts, PSN is tailored to particular communities to strategically address specific violent crime and public safety challenges. As a key component of Operation Take Back America, PSN serves a central role in the Department’s commitment to make our country safe. PSN emphasizes three core principles: rapid federal response to violent crime and criminal offenders; strong, strategic partnerships among law enforcement at all levels; and accountability and deterrence through the prosecution of the most serious, readily provable offenses and other strategies. These efforts complement and strengthen President Trump’s Homeland Security Task Forces, ensuring a comprehensive federal response to the most pressing public safety issues facing communities.
title: St. Louis County Felon Admits Being Caught with Guns in Stolen Car After Shootout, Chase

SIOUX FALLS - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that Chief United States District Court Judge Roberto A. Lange has sentenced a Sioux Falls, South Dakota, man convicted of Attempted Enticement of a Minor Using the Internet. The sentencing took place on September 14, 2026.

Ryan Nigro, age 34, was sentenced to 10 years in federal prison, five years of supervised release, and a special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund in the amount of $100. Upon release from federal prison, Nigro must register as a sex offender for 25 years.

Nigro was indicted by a federal grand jury in April 2024. He was found guilty at a jury trial on June 4, 2026.

The conviction stemmed from an undercover chat operation in which several law enforcement agencies worked together to identify individuals using the Internet to attempt to have sex with children. In this case, Nigro used the application Reddit to start a conversation with a person he believed was a 12-year-old girl. Nigro introduced the topic of sex into the conversation and asked the child to meet with him at a local hotel for sex. Nigro arrived at the hotel where he was arrested by law enforcement. The 12-year-old female persona was operated by a special agent with Homeland Security Investigations.

This case was investigated by the Homeland Security Investigations, the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force (ICAC), South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, Sioux Falls Police Department, Watertown Police Department, Tea Police Department, Rapid City Police Department, Minnehaha County Sheriff’s Office, Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, and South Dakota Highway Patrol. Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth E. Ebert-Webb prosecuted the case.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc .

Nigro was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.
title: Sioux Falls Man Sentenced to 10 Years in Federal Prison for Attempted Enticement of a Minor Using the Internet

Russian National Sentenced for Synthetic Identity Theft Fraud Scheme and Conspiring to Submit Fraudulent Voter Registrations
Dmitry Shushlebin, 45, a Russian citizen living in Miami Beach, Florida, was sentenced to six years in prison and three years of supervised release for organizing an identity theft fraud scheme that included efforts by the conspirators to submit fraudulent voter registrations.He was also ordered to pay $458,839.69 in restitution.
“Those who engage in fraud and deception in our election processes will be investigated and prosecuted,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “After arriving in the United States, Dmitry Shushlebin created sham companies to facilitate a multi-year financial fraud scheme. He used these companies to commit identity theft, which allowed him to create synthetic or fake identities that appeared real after they were used to submit over 100 false voter registrations.”
“Voting is one of the most significant rights and responsibilities Americans have,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We will continue to investigate threats to the integrity of our electoral process and prosecute those who engage in fraud or other means to violate our nation’s voting laws.”
“The FBI is committed to supporting our election security partners ensuring fraudulent schemes, like the defendant’s identity-theft scheme using fraudulent voter registration applications, never have a chance to succeed,” said Special Agent in Charge Rodney Crawford of the FBI Tampa Division. “We have the investigative tools and the strong partnerships to detect and disrupt these crimes.”
“Combatting fraud and identity theft are critical missions of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service” said Inspector in Charge Bladismir Rojo of the U.S. Postal Inspection Service Miami Division. “We will continue to work with our local, state, and federal partners to investigate those individuals who use the mail to enrich themselves at the expense of others.”
On July 24, 2025, the United States filed a four-count superseding information charging Shushlebin with conspiracy to give false information in registering to vote and submit fraudulent voter registrations, wire fraud, making false statements, and aggravated identity theft. Shushlebin pleaded guilty to all four counts on July 25, 2025.
According to court documents, Shushlebin hired Sanjar Jamilov, an Uzbekistani national, and others to submit more than 100 fraudulent voter registration applications to the Pinellas County Supervisor of Elections in February and March 2023. One purpose of registering these fake voters was to create synthetic or fake identities that Shushlebin could use to commit financial fraud. Shushlebin used the fake identities to obtain fraudulent credit cards and loans. He perpetrated this scheme against the victim financial institutions hundreds of times using hundreds of different synthetic identities.
The FBI investigated this case with assistance from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service.
Acting Chief Edward P. Sullivan of the Criminal Division’s Public Integrity Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Lindsey Schmidt for the Middle District of Florida are prosecuting the case. Former Assistant U.S. Attorney Daniel Marcet for the Middle District of Florida and Public Integrity Section Trial Attorney Leo Wise provided substantial assistance with the investigation and prosecution.
title: Russian National Sentenced for Synthetic Identity Theft Fraud Scheme and Conspiring to Submit Fraudulent Voter Registrations

Today, Congresswoman Suzan DelBene (WA-01) forced a vote on an amendment during a Ways & Means Committee markup that would require the Trump administration to release yet-unseen information about the WISeR program. The program pays private companies to use AI to delay and deny care to seniors in Washington and five other states.

Since the program began in January, patients have been left in severe pain and unable to access the care prescribed by their doctors. In June, DelBene announced that Virtix, the company administering WISeR in Washington, was ordered to submit a corrective action plan for delays in reviewing claims after a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) audit of its performance. Neither document has been released to Congress or the public.

The amendment would force CMS to release any audits or corrective action plans for WISeR-participating companies within 3 months. It would also direct the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission to analyze the impacts of Medicare Advantage plans’ red tape on patients and providers. Ways & Means Republicans rejected the amendment by an 18-19 vote.

“It’s clear why the administration is doing everything they can to conceal these documents. The more that Americans learn about WISeR, the more outraged they get at the Trump administration for jeopardizing their care and trying to privatize Medicare,” said DelBene.

This effort was informed by a bombshell report released by the Electronic Frontier Foundation that revealed widespread delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm. The report contains nearly 1,000 pages of documentation, including contracts with participating companies, internal reports, and health care providers’ complaints about the program, that were obtained through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request and lawsuit. It also sheds light on the CMS’ plan to expand WISeR to cancer treatments and other types of care.

DelBene introduced legislation last November to repeal WISeR and has led multiple other legislative efforts to stop the program.
title: Ways & Means Republicans Continue Covering Up Harms of Trump’s Medicare AI Experiment

text:
Transcript of Stanton, McGovern, Khanna, Pelosi, and Moulton Opening Statements From Shadow Hearing on Human Rights in China Ahead of Xi’s Visit to Washington
WASHINGTON – On Tuesday, the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party Minority and Congressional-Executive Commission on China Ranking Member Jim McGovern held a hearing titled The Void in China Policy: Why Human Rights Must Be on Trump’s Agenda with Xi at the White House.
The following witnesses provided testimony:
- Tahir Imin, Founder and Director, Uyghur Post
- Palden Gyal, President, International Tibet Media Organization
- Yaqiu Wang, Fellow at the Penn Project on the Future of U.S.-China Relations at the University of Pennsylvania
- Jonathan Stivers, U.S. Director, Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong; Commissioner, U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission’
Below is a transcript of opening statements delivered by Representative Greg Stanton, CECC Ranking Member McGovern, Ranking Member Khanna, Speaker Emerita Pelosi, and Representative Seth Moulton. A recording of the hearing can be found here.
First off, I want to acknowledge this gentleman sitting next to me. His entire career has been just one of the strongest voices in Congress, arguably in America, for human rights around the globe. So, thank you for your steadfast and consistent leadership.
And the gentleman on my left, who is currently the ranking member of the Select Committee on China, because of the change in times and votes, he originally wasn't supposed to be here, but now he's able to be here. So, you get two of us from the Committee, so good to see you. Thank you, Ro Khanna.
Thank you, Ranking Member McGovern, for your strong remarks and for co-chairing today's hearing on human rights abuses in the People's Republic of China.
More than three and a half years ago, the Select Committee held its second hearing after being established. The second hearing of the Select Committee was particularly on the Chinese Communist Party's abuses of the Uyghur people.
And today in 2026, that persecution continues.
In January, a group of UN human rights experts alleged that the Chinese Communist Party continues to subject its Uyghur, Tibetan, and other minority populations to forced labor, using “coercive elements so severe that they may amount to enslavement and a crime against humanity.”
Beginning in 2017, the CCP arbitrarily detained more than a million ethnic Uyghurs and other Muslims in “re-education facilities,” which are just concentration camps.
In these camps, parents are forcibly separated from their children. Children are sent to state-run boarding schools where they are systematically stripped of their native language, culture, and religious heritage.
Adult detainees are subjected to political indoctrination, sexual violence, forced female sterilization and abortions, food deprivation, and other forms of torture. They are forced to renounce Islam as a condition for their release.
This direction comes straight from the top. A CCP religious affairs official said in 2017 about the Uyghurs: the Chinese government will “break their lineage, break their roots, break their connections, and break their origins.”
Unfortunately, the CCP's severe repression is not isolated to Xinjiang.
In 2024, 650,000 Tibetans were forced from the homes as part of a CCP program to systematically transfer what it called “rural surplus labor.”
Since 2000, it is estimated that almost 3.5 million Tibetans have been forced from their homes by the CCP, including through what are called "old village relocation" programs.
In 1963, images of a Buddhist monk setting himself on fire to protest the South Vietnamese government shocked the conscience of our world. Since 2009, at least 170 Tibetans have self-immolated to protest the CCP's repression.
We have to ask ourselves: where is the conscience of our world today?
Next week, President Trump will roll out the red carpet for Xi Jinping, honoring him with a state dinner at the White House. Unfortunately, the Trump administration has not shown much of a willingness to confront Xi about his horrific human rights abuses.
This starts with President Trump himself, who, according to two former officials in the administration, encouraged Xi's creation of concentration camps in Xinjiang, telling Xi it was "exactly the right thing to do."
A senior Trump official who for a time was the acting president of the United States Institute of Peace blamed Uyghurs for the CCP's atrocities against them, saying that "the Chinese aren't genocidal, they just object to Uyghur-ness.”
Meanwhile, the Trump administration has attempted to pull the rug out from under human rights groups that are pushing back against the CCP’s abuses. They slashed funding and grants for human rights organizations, gutted the State Department's human rights bureaus, and tried to shutter groups that empower human rights defenders in China, like the National Endowment for Democracy and Radio Free Asia.
President Trump has called Xi Jinping a “friend” and a “incredible man who has done amazing things.” It is unbefitting any leader of a great country to use words like that to describe someone who has oppressed the human rights and dignity of others.
Standing up for the oppressed in the PRC, whether it be Uyghurs, Tibetans, Hong Kongers, Mongolians, or Han Chinese has always been and must be a bipartisan issue.
Chairman, Co-Chair, we have incredible witnesses today. People who have shown unbelievable courage. We are inspired by you, your actions, what you're doing to support the people you represent. It's incredible.
I look forward to hearing from these incredible witnesses today on what more Congress can do and should do to hold the CCP accountable for its human rights abuses and stand up for all those who are oppressed by its autocratic rule.
We convene this hearing to shine a light on the severe violations of human rights by the government of China, and to assess our government's performance in holding it accountable. 
Human rights in China has long been an area of bipartisan concern and productivity here in the Congress.
I think of Congresswoman Nancy Pelosi standing in Tiananmen Square with Republican and Democratic colleagues in 1991, bravely unfurling a banner to the victims of the massacre before being whisked away by police.
I think of President George W. Bush and the bipartisan House and Senate leadership in 2007 presenting the Congressional Gold Medal to His Holiness the Dalai Lama.
I think of Marco Rubio and myself as co-chairs of the CECC, working together to craft and pass the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act of 2021 into law.
I think of institutions we created to monitor the Chinese government's behavior, the CECC, Select Committee, the U.S. Security and Economic Review Commission – and we welcome one of its commissioners today as a witness.
There has been consensus that U.S. policy toward China must include a moral dimension; that we must speak out for the freedoms of those who cannot advocate for themselves. That we must deploy policy tools to press the Chinese government to respect human rights.
That consensus, I fear, is disappearing – and here is why:
President Trump has removed human rights from U.S. foreign policy in favor of a transactional approach.
President Trump carried no human rights agenda to Beijing, other than to ask to free two individuals – individuals we care deeply about – only one of which succeeded.
Secretary Rubio decimated the State Department's Human Rights Bureau and cut grants to China human rights organizations.
The Administration wants to eliminate Radio Free Asia and Voice of America, among the only sources of independent information for those living under the Chinese censorship regime.
These actions take us backwards. They undermine so much that Republicans and Democrats have worked to build up over the years.
But rather than defend the tools that helped us promote human rights in China, the Republican majority in Congress sat on their hands, and the numbers back this up.
When Biden was president, the CECC averaged 15 hearings and 23 advocacy letters per Congress. With Trump as president, the CECC has scheduled only seven hearings and sent out only three letters.
Between 2018 and 2024, Congress passed the Reciprocal Access to Tibet Act, the Tibetan Policy and Support Act, the Promoting a Resolution to the Tibet-China Dispute Act, the Uyghur Human Rights Policy Act, the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act, the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, the Hong Kong Autonomy Act, and the Protect Hong Kong Act – all bipartisan measures.
This Congress has not sent one single China human rights bill to the president. Not one. And at the same time, our Republican colleagues are removing the words "human rights" and references to international human rights treaties from bills and resolutions.
And here's an example: the House and the Senate passed resolutions calling for the release of Jimmy Lai. That’s good. But neither frames his case in human rights language. Neither mentions China's legally binding international human rights obligations that could be leveraged to secure his freedom.
That omission does a disservice to the cause that Jimmy has gone to jail to defend.
In my service on the CECC and as co-chair of the Tom Lantos Human Rights Commission, I have closely monitored human rights conditions in China. And make no mistake: the Chinese government remains one of the world's worst abusers of its own people.
We have a moral obligation to speak out and to take action for those who suffer under this repression. But it is a real question whether the U.S. has the moral credibility to call on Chinese authorities to approve human rights.
At the CECC, we report on how the Chinese government prosecutes journalists and political opponents of the of the ruling party, restricts freedom of expression and assembly, puts ethnic minorities in detention facilities, engages in arbitrary detention, and commits extrajudicial killings.
But today, here in the United States, under the current administration, our own government, is committing each of the same violations, from the streets of Minneapolis to the Caribbean Sea. Our own government is murdering people in cold blood.
Uyghurs, Hong Kongers, and Chinese fled persecution in China and sought refuge in the United States. Now, our own government is detaining them and sending them to ICE facilities with the intention to deport them to a dark fate.
I have publicly condemned this policy, but I don't know of a single one of my colleagues on the other side of the aisle who has had the courage to publicly criticize this president for this abuse, and I think that that's cowardly.
The United States is rapidly forfeiting the high ground to speak against human rights violations in China or any other place on the globe.
Why should anyone trust the word of an abuser when they tell others abuse is wrong?
And I close by quoting Speaker Emerita Pelosi, who has said to presidents of both parties, both parties. I mean, I've seen her tough on Republicans. I've seen her tough on Democrats. And her quote is: "If we do not speak out for human rights in China because of commercial interests, we lose all moral authority to speak out for human rights anywhere.”
That call is more relevant today than ever and I am anxiously waiting to see how President Xi is treated when he comes to this country and what he is pressed on. Is it just commercial interest? Or is human rights going to be front and center on the agenda?
Thank you, Chairman, for your leadership on this for so many years.
There's no one who has stood up for human rights in China and around the world more than Jim McGovern. And this was his idea, his initiative to have the China Committee – Select Committee do this, and I'm really grateful to you.
I also want to thank Representative Stanton. I had a personal commitment with my family, and he stepped in to help chair it, and I appreciate that.
Of course, we have our illustrious Speaker Emerita here. I'm sure Jim McGovern will recognize her, but she showed so much courage. Has shown so much courage on this issue. We share representation in the Bay Area, and by share, I mean I'm geographically close to her.
And I'll tell you, there's a huge Chinese American community in my district, huge Chinese American community in her district. The easy thing for her to do, politically, would have just been to go along and not speak out on human rights, and it was extraordinarily courageous, politically courageous, for her to take the stances that she has taken her whole career.
I would just say that President Biden, as Seth Moulton said, really made this a priority. We actually had sanctions on products made by the Uyghurs. We actually were enforcing the law.
Donald Trump, for all his rhetoric about fair trade and making sure that American manufacturers aren't going to be shafted, and making sure that we're going to rebalance with China has totally dropped the ball on this issue. So, I appreciate Congressman McGovern, our chair, bringing this back to our attention.
As I’ve said to you when we've been on our CODELS to Tibet and China and all the rest: you [Congressman McGovern] are our spiritual leader in all of this. Completely values-based, committed, prioritizing this as a highly important initiative for us all to be involved in, and I’ve worked on this for a long time.
I see Jonathan Stivers, who was on my staff, for part of that.
I also want to welcome Palden Gyal from Tibet, Yaqiu Wang of the [Penn Project] on the Future of U.S.-China Relations, and Tahir Imin.
Here are a couple things. I have said over and over again: if we do not speak up for human rights in China because of commercial interest, we lose all moral authority to speak up for human rights any place in the world. And apparently, we seem to be abdicating that right.
Uyghurs – a genocide going on with the Uyghurs. In terms of democracy in Hong Kong, terrible in terms of repression. Just to commemorate what happened in Tiananmen Square, you got seven years in prison, at least. So the list goes on. And just all of the other violations of human rights in China.
So thank you for giving us a chance to call to attention, because what they’ve said, with a government like the Chinese government, one of the most excruciating forms of their torture is to tell the prisoners, “nobody even remembers you. They don't even know what you did or why you're in prison. Why don't you just confess?”
We want to put lie to that. We always want to mention, whether we're delivering letters, whether we're speaking on the floor, whatever it is, to make sure that people in prison know that they are not forgotten, that their courage is recognized, and we will not rest until there is some justice in all of this.
So, thank you again. And I thank Mr. Khanna for his kind words and thank you for the leadership that you're providing now on the Committee as well. I'm so pleased to hear that. And thank you again, our spiritual leader [Mr. McGovern].
Serving on the Select Committee on China – the full name of the committee is the Select Committee on Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party.
The verb there is competition. And the competition between the United States and China is not just for economic dominance or military dominance; it's for leadership, and it comes down to not just which country is stronger, but which country has the values that the rest of the world wants to follow.
That's really what's at stake: who will lead the world, not just from power, but values.
China under Xi Jinping has spent the past decade and a half systematically eroding the rights of everyone living in China. For most of that time, the United States has pushed back in a strongly bipartisan manner.
We engaged on the genocide of Uyghurs in one of the most effective pieces of legislating the U.S. Congress has ever done on a human rights issue with the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act.
And then under this presidency, we stopped trying. This administration has canceled dozens of grant programs supporting civil society, pro-democracy programming, and independent journalism that were actively undermining the CCP's efforts to suppress independent thought in China.
This administration is uniquely good at shooting themselves in the foot. But the decision to gut the U.S. Agency for Global Media was, even for them, a historically tragic decision.
This is an institution that, for a very small amount of money, dramatically shaped the world's information environment in ways that align with both U.S. values and the truth.
My colleagues on the Select Committee have often heard me harp on the fact that while “competition” is the verb and the title, the first order of business in our relationship with China today is deterrence. It's to prevent a war, a war that Xi Jinping has made very clear he is ready and willing to start.
We think about deterrence usually in just military terms, but if you ask the Pentagon about deterrence, they'll tell you that there are four elements: there's military, economic, diplomatic, and information.
We understand the importance of military power. We understand the importance of economic power. But in that information realm, we have to tell our story. We can't cut off the very organisms of our government that are designed to do that and tell a better story, not just to the world but to the people in China today.
And on diplomacy, that brings us back to where I began: the question of moral leadership. Who will be the next great superpower leader of the world? The question, not just of power, but of values. This administration seems to throw those values out the window. It's critical we get them back. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
title: Transcript of Stanton, McGovern, Khanna, Pelosi, and Moulton Opening Statements From Shadow Hearing on Human Rights in China Ahead of Xi’s Visit to Washington

PIERRE - United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced today that U.S. District Judge Eric C. Schulte has sentenced a Murdo, South Dakota, man convicted of Assault Resulting in Serious Bodily Injury. The sentencing took place on September 14, 2026.

Dane Menard, age 20, was sentenced to two years and six months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Menard was indicted by a federal grand jury in August 2025. He pleaded guilty on June 15, 2026.

The conviction stems from an incident that occurred in an area of Mellette County, South Dakota, that is part of the Rosebud Sioux Indian Reservation. On March 15, 2025, Menard struck the victim, an adult male, with his vehicle in the driveway of a residence near White River, South Dakota. The victim was hospitalized with injuries that included a broken arm and broken ankle.

This matter is being prosecuted by the U.S. Attorney’s Office because the Major Crimes Act, a federal statute, mandates that certain violent crimes alleged to have occurred in Indian country be prosecuted in federal court as opposed to State court.

This case was investigated by the Rosebud Sioux Tribe Law Enforcement Services. Supervisory Assistant U.S. Attorney Kirk Albertson prosecuted the case.

Menard was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.
title: Murdo Man Sentenced for Assault Resulting in Serious Bodily Injury

ICE expands local 287(g) law enforcement partnerships in Tennessee
NASHVILLE, Tenn. — ICE is expanding its state and local law enforcement partnerships across Tennessee, strengthening cooperation to identify and remove criminal illegal aliens who pose public safety threats.
As of Sept. 9, ICE has 120 of these 287(g) partners in Tennessee. Participating agencies may operate under the Jail Enforcement, Warrant Service Officer and Task Force models. Across the country, ICE has signed 2,466 memoranda of agreement with 287(g) partners.
“287(g) is a critical public safety initiative that gives law enforcement agencies another tool to protect their communities,” said ICE Public Safety Partnership Division Assistant Director Russell Hott. “By working closely with sheriffs, chiefs and our state partners across Tennessee, law enforcement is able to apprehend criminal illegal aliens who continue to prey on and victimize local communities and remove those threats from our neighborhoods.”
The 287(g) program is an invaluable resource that provides state and local law enforcement agencies with another tool to enhance public safety in their communities by arresting and removing criminal illegal aliens involved in gang activity, violent crimes, sex offenses, drug trafficking and numerous other forms of illicit activity. Since Jan. 20, 2025, ICE enforcement activity in the state has included more than 1,300 arrests by 287(g) partners and 542 encounters with aliens in local custody.
Last month, the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office became an operational 287(g) partner and arrested Reniery Garcia-Godoy, a criminal illegal alien from Honduras, on the first day of the partnership. Garcia-Godoy, who was taken into custody near the Tennessee-Alabama state line, had two felony convictions for sexual battery in Franklin, Tennessee, and has since been removed from the U.S.
Other public safety threats arrested by 287(g) partners and transferred to ICE custody include:
These criminal illegal aliens remain in ICE custody pending immigration proceedings.
“Partnerships like these are essential to public safety,” said ERO New Orleans acting Field Office Director Scott Ladwig. “The continued expansion of 287(g) in Tennessee demonstrates the commitment of ICE and our law enforcement partners to remove dangerous criminal aliens from our communities.”
ERO New Orleans officials and ICE’s Public Safety Partnership Division recently attended the Tennessee Sheriffs’ Association Conference to meet with sheriffs and other law enforcement leaders about the program. Earlier this year, Tennessee passed a law requiring all sheriffs’ offices to enter into a 287(g) agreement by Jan. 1, 2027. Agencies that do not comply could lose certain state funding.
Seven out of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE. For more information about the 287(g) program, visit ICE.gov.
Under President Trump, Secretary Mullin and acting ICE Director David J. Venturella, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Criminal illegal aliens are unwelcome in the U.S.
title: ICE expands local 287(g) law enforcement partnerships in Tennessee

Following the Major Richard Star Act’s discharge petition hitting its necessary 218 signatures, Congressman Chris Pappas (NH-01), a member of the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee (HVAC) and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, released the following statement:

“It’s past time to eliminate the ‘wounded veteran tax’ that reduces the benefits that our veterans earn with their service and sacrifice,” said Congressman Pappas. "We're working hard to get this across the finish line and see it become law before the end of the year, and I’m thrilled to see our discharge petition reach 218 signatures. I thank our veterans for speaking out and for their leadership on this issue. We’re making sure Congress steps up and does our part by forcing a vote in the House, and we’ll keep fighting until this bill finally becomes law.”

Pappas was the third member to sign a discharge petition for the Major Richard Star Act, and has been a cosponsor every Congress since being elected in 2019. This legislation currently has 330 cosponsors and would end the “wounded veteran tax”, or the offset that keeps medically retired veterans from receiving their full Department of Defense retirement pay and their full Veterans Affairs disability pay. The discharge petition was filed by House Committee on Veterans’ Affairs Ranking Member Mark Takano (CA-39) and Congressman Raul Ruiz (CA-25).

"218 signatures means the House has spoken. A majority of members, Democrats and Republicans, said enough is enough," said Ranking Member Takano. "Combat-injured veterans shouldn't have to choose between the retirement they earned and the disability compensation they're owed. The time for that debate is over. The only person standing between these veterans and their money now is Speaker Johnson, and he's out of excuses."

"It's official—we did it! We reached 218 signatures, and veterans just won a floor vote on my bipartisan Major Richard Star Act," said Congressman Ruiz. "While this is a victory worth celebrating, the fight continues to deliver justice for our veterans, who for years have lived with the injustice of being forced to medically retire due to combat-related injuries, penalized and unable to receive both their disability compensation and their retirement pay in full. Now, the real work begins with this bipartisan bill, it is time for Congress to show our veterans that their sacrifice was not in vain and that we are here to support them."

The Major Richard Star Act is supported by Veterans of Foreign Wars, The American Legion, Wounded Warrior Project, Disabled American Veterans, and Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America, and a number of other Veterans Service Organizations.
title: Pappas-Backed Major Richard Star Act Discharge Petition Hits 218, Forces Vote to Correct Injustice for Veterans

Washington, D.C. — The following are opening remarks, as prepared for delivery, from Ranking Member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure Rick Larsen (D-WA) and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Salud Carbajal (D-CA) during today’s Subcommittee hearing titled “Always Ready: A Day in the Life of a United States Coast Guard Member.”
Video of Ranking Members Larsen’s and Carbajal’s opening statements can be found here and here.
More information on the hearing can be found here.
Ranking Member Larsen:
Thank you, Chairman Ezell and Ranking Member Carbajal, for holding today’s hearing.
Before we get started, I want to take moment to honor Lieutenant Connor Overstreet who recently lost his life to a senseless act of gun violence in my state.
This loss hits close to home as he attended flight school with my son. Lieutenant Overstreet was a dedicated helicopter pilot who joined the service to help others. My condolences go out to his family and friends for their loss.
Joining us in the audience, we have enlisted members of the Coast Guard who have traveled from across the country to be here today. Before the hearing, Members of this subcommittee had the opportunity to hear directly from these servicemembers and get their unique perspectives on what it means to be a Coastie, and, let me tell you, they’re impressive individuals.
Each of you are vital to the Coast Guard’s success in securing our waters and saving lives. The country is in your debt.
Hearing directly from enlisted personnel is incredibly helpful as this Committee works to improve the Coast Guard and the lives of servicemembers.
There are over 30,000 enlisted Coast Guard personnel. These dedicated individuals play a crucial role in responding to emergencies, enforcing laws and protecting natural resources.
Coast Guard members serve our country with distinction, and it is our responsibility to ensure they have the resources they need.
This includes affordable housing, essential health services, accessible childcare centers and up-to-date cutters, aircraft and technology.
In fiscal year 2023, the Coast Guard faced a nearly 3,000 personnel shortfall but in recent years has nearly closed that gap.
It is not enough, however, to recruit new servicemembers, we need to retain them. Once joining the service, enlisted Coasties continue to face substandard housing options, working conditions, a lack of available healthcare and affordable childcare.
Due to the unique mission of the Service, Coast Guard stations are often in remote or high-cost coastal areas.
The stress of expensive housing takes a toll on servicemember well-being and overall readiness.
Limited Coast Guard owned housing and the Department of Defense’s Basic Allowance for Housing, which does not appropriately consider Coast Guard locations, forces personnel to find more affordable housing with longer commutes.
The availability of providers accepting TRICARE and the quality of care is inconsistent in many remote areas where the Coast Guard operates. Personnel face unacceptably long wait times for appointments and limited access to specialized care.
Not only does the Coast Guard face unique operating environments, Coasties also face unique health problems associated with service.
A recent New York Times article highlighted the high risk of traumatic brain injuries in boat crew and a history of inaction on the issue by Coast Guard leadership. This is unacceptable, and Coasties deserve better.
The link between traumatic brain injuries, mental health and suicide is clear.
According to the Coast Guard Foundation, in 2022, Coast Guard members died from suicide twice as often as their peers in other military services. Investing in mental health is not just a moral obligation, it is critical for maintaining operational readiness.
Recently, Ranking Member Carbajal and I sent a letter to the Coast Guard pushing an independent review of how to improve monitoring and preventing of traumatic brain injury in boat crews.
Many enlisted personnel are parents who juggle demanding work schedules with family responsibilities.
Servicemembers often have difficulty finding affordable and reliable childcare which directly impacts their ability to do their jobs.
While funding was provided in the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law to build four new Child Development Centers in remote areas, the Coast Guard has struggled with staffing.
This limits the number of children who can enroll and forces members to look elsewhere for childcare—something very difficult to find in remote areas. 
In order to do their job, members of the Coast Guard need the right tools.
I am closely monitoring the Coast Guard’s procurement of new assets and systems through last year’s reconciliation funding. While the replacement of aging assets is long overdue, the Coast Guard simply doesn’t have the shoreside infrastructure required to support those assets. 
In its adoption of new technology, the Coast Guard must prioritize servicemembers.
We have a responsibility to ensure that those who dedicate their lives to protecting Americans receive the resources and support they need to thrive both on and off duty.
I have seen firsthand the challenges our Coasties are facing, and I am glad we are taking the time to discuss it today.
Thank you, and I yield back.
Ranking Member Carbajal:
Good afternoon, Chair Ezell, and thank you for holding today’s hearing.
The Coast Guard asks a great deal of its people. Servicemembers are expected to answer the call at a moment’s notice, operate in some of the most challenging environments in the country, and carry out dangerous missions that protect American lives, our communities and our economic security.
Today, we have an opportunity to put the people behind those missions front and center.
Over the years, I have visited Coast Guard units across the country to see their work up close. Those visits have given me an even greater appreciation for the professionalism, skill and commitment that Coasties bring to the job every day.
The missions they perform are essential.
Coast Guard personnel conduct search and rescue, interdict illegal drugs, protect our marine environment, safeguard our fisheries, and help ensure that our maritime transportation system remains safe and secure. They do this while operating around the clock and often far from home.
That is an extraordinary responsibility, and it demands an extraordinary workforce.
As Ranking Member of this Subcommittee, I am proud to be an advocate for the Coast Guard. But being an advocate means more than recognizing the importance of the mission. It means making sure the people responsible for carrying out that mission have what they need to succeed.
That starts with the basics.
A servicemember should always be able to find a safe and affordable place to live.
I know that this is challenging given that 41 percent of Coast Guard units are located in some of the most remote and expensive areas of the United States.
I have seen this challenge firsthand in my own district on the Central Coast of California, where Coast Guard families have faced both the high cost of housing and unacceptable conditions in Coast Guard-provided housing.
I personally visited Coast Guard housing in Santa Barbara twice after learning about serious problems, including mold, persistent water issues, and deteriorating floors. In fact, one Coast Guard member fell through a shower floor because moisture and mold had caused the floor to deteriorate.
No servicemember should have to choose between paying more than they can afford to live near their duty station and living in housing that is unsafe or unhealthy.
And this is not simply a quality-of-life issue.
When Coast Guard members cannot afford to live near their units—or when the housing provided to them is not safe—it can directly affect readiness, morale and the Service's ability to retain the people it needs.
For the families stationed in these communities, the cost of serving can extend well beyond the demands of the job itself. Housing costs can make living near a duty station unrealistic.
Long commutes can take valuable time away from family.
Access to medical care can require significant travel. And, finding affordable childcare can be especially difficult for families whose schedules do not fit the traditional nine-to-five workday.
We need to recognize these challenges for what they are: readiness issues.
When a Coast Guard member is worried about whether their family can make rent, whether their child has access to daycare, or whether their family can see a doctor, that affects morale.
It affects quality of life and overtime. It can affect whether talented people choose to join the Service or whether experienced members decide to stay.
We cannot ask Coast Guard personnel to make extraordinary sacrifices while overlooking the everyday challenges facing their families.
That is why continued investment in the Coast Guard workforce is so important. New cutters, aircraft, facilities, and other capabilities are critical, but those investments only deliver results if we have trained and experienced people available to operate them.
Recruitment and retention are inseparable from the investments we make in our Coast Guard families.
Every Coast Guard mission starts and ends with people.
I look forward to hearing directly from our witnesses today about what Coast Guard personnel are experiencing, where the greatest challenges are, and what Congress can do to address them.
The men and women of the Coast Guard have demonstrated time and time again that they will be there when America needs them.
Our responsibility is to make sure America is there for them.
Thank you, Chair Ezell. I yield back.
--30--
title: Ranking Members Larsen, Carbajal Statements from Hearing on Coast Guard Quality of Life

WASHINGTON – The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), in coordination with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), will conduct a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System (EAS) on Tuesday, November 17, 2026.
FEMA’s Emergency Alert System is a national public warning system made up of thousands of radio, television, cable, satellite and wireline video providers. Through the Emergency Alert System, the President can address the American people or share life-saving information with the public during a national emergency. FEMA is required by law to conduct a nationwide test of the public alert and warning system at least once every three years. These tests allow FEMA to identify technical or operational issues before the system is needed during an actual emergency.
FEMA and the FCC are sharing the test date in advance because it is important that the public understands what to expect on the day of the test. At approximately 2:20 p.m. ET on November 17, 2026, radio and television broadcasters, cable systems, satellite radio and television providers, and wireline video providers nationwide will interrupt normal programming to relay a test message. This message will state, “This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, covering the United States from 2:20 to 2:50 hours ET. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.” When the test has concluded, normal programming will resume.
FEMA and the FCC are coordinating with stakeholders, including participating communications providers as well as federal, state, tribal and territorial agencies, to prepare for and conduct the test.
More information about Emergency Alert System is available on FEMA.gov.
title: FEMA and FCC Schedule 2026 Nationwide Test of the Emergency Alert System for November 17, 2026

text:
ATF investigation results in a 12-year sentence for Gastonia drug trafficker
CHARLOTTE, N.C. – A joint ATF, Gaston County Police Department led investigation resulted in a 12-year sentence for Bryan Tromon Green, 35, of Gastonia, N.C. Green was sentenced on Wednesday for distributing fentanyl-laced pills and selling firearms in Gaston County.
“The combination of drug dealing and illegal firearm possession is a recipe for violence and tragedy,” said ATF Special Agent in Charge Alicia Jones. “Taking back firearms from prohibited individuals and stopping the flow of drugs into our communities is a priority for ATF and all of our law enforcement partners.”
Green’s co-conspirator, Jarvis Sentell Lynn, 38, also of Gastonia, was previously sentenced to more than nine years in prison for trafficking fentanyl and cocaine.
Between March 2024 and April 2024, Green, a convicted felon, sold fentanyl pills multiple times to a confidential informant in Gaston County. The same informant also purchased two firearms from Green: a Walther, Model PK380, .380 caliber semi-automatic pistol and an American Tactical Imports, Model Omni Hybrid, 5.56 caliber semi-automatic rifle.
During that same period, law enforcement also set up multiple controlled drug purchases with co-conspirator Lynn at his residence in Gastonia for pills pressed with fentanyl. Investigators were able to purchase a firearm from Lynn and later seized multiple weapons and ammunition from his residence, including semi-automatic pistols and rifles.
Green and Lynn both pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl and cocaine and distribution of fentanyl. They are in federal custody and will be transferred to the custody of the Federal Bureau of Prisons upon designation to a federal facility.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Nick J. Miller of the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Charlotte prosecuted the case.
###
ATF protects American communities from violent crime driven by the illegal use of firearms, explosives, and acts of arson. Through crime gun intelligence, forensic analysis, and relentless investigation, we identify and arrest violent offenders and gang members, dismantle trafficking networks, and sever the supply chains arming cartels, prohibited persons, and terrorist organizations. We defend the rights of law-abiding citizens by safeguarding lawful commerce and upholding the Constitution of the United States. Learn more about what ATF is doing to reduce violent crime in your community by following us on X @ATFHQ, Instagram @ATFHQ, LinkedIn @ATF, and Facebook @HQATF, or on the web at www.atf.gov.
title: ATF investigation results in a 12-year sentence for Gastonia drug trafficker

For more than six months, the Trump Administration has waged war in Iran without Congressional approval, costing Americans more than $100 billion, killing 18 brave U.S. servicemembers, and wounding hundreds more

Ryan has voted to end the war six times, with a third consecutive vote passing the House last night with bipartisan support

Ryan’s No Funds for Iran War Act – which prohibits the use of additional taxpayer funds for the war in Iran – has also gained steady support and now has more than 60 cosponsors

Ryan has been the leading voice of opposition to Trump’s war in Iran; he sits on the House Armed Services Committee, is the first West Point graduate to represent the Academy in Congress, and served two combat tours in Iraq earning him two Bronze Stars

WASHINGTON, DC – Following last night’s vote to pass a third War Powers Resolution to end President Trump’s war in Iran, Congressman Pat Ryan announced growing support for his No Funds for Iran War Act, legislation to prohibit the use of additional taxpayer dollars on Trump’s war without Congressional approval. The bill now has more than 60 cosponsors.

Ryan – an Iraq War combat veteran and the first West Point graduate to represent the Academy in Congress – has voted to end Trump’s war in Iran six separate times, with each vote gaining bipartisan support. The resolution last night passed the House of Representatives for a third consecutive time by a vote of 220-204. Trump’s war has now killed 18 brave U.S. troops, injured more than 800, and raised prices across the board on the American people.

More than six months into the war with Iran, Ryan is encouraging his colleagues not to give up the fight, and urging Members across the aisle to listen to their constituents and join his efforts to stop the war.

“Every single American – from the military families with loved ones deployed overseas, to the farmer buying fertilizer to feed our communities, to the mom filling up her gas tank – is feeling the impact of this reckless war with Iran. The American people want this war to end – and it's past time for Trump, Hegseth, and all their allies in Congress to listen,” said Congressman Pat Ryan. “Every time we force my Republican colleagues to face the facts, more and more of them vote with us. We’ve now voted three times, in a bipartisan way, to end the war. But Trump continues to ignore the will of the people. My bill to prohibit the use of more taxpayer dollars now has more than 60 cosponsors and would cut off his recklessness at the source. The dam is breaking – we have to keep up the pressure. I’m going to keep fighting everyday, with every fiber of my being, to end this war and bring our troops home.”

According to a new report from the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Trump’s war in Iran has caused more than 40 percent of inflation from the second quarter of 2026 and will continue to drive inflation higher into 2027, meaning the cost of basic goods will continue to rise. CBO also stated the U.S. military will not be able to replace munitions for at least five years.

A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll found that 61 percent of Americans believe using military force against Iran was a mistake, making Trump’s war as unpopular among Americans as the Iraq War during the peak of violence in 2006 and the Vietnam War in the early 1970s.

The Pentagon’s internal overall cost estimate has exceeded $100 billion. That number doesn’t even account for the cost to the American people. Gas prices have soared, as people across NY‐18 have spent an additional $172 million on gas since the beginning of the war, costing the average family in our district an additional $646 in gas costs over the past six months. Grocery prices have also skyrocketed as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed.

Ryan has repeatedly cosponsored and voted in favor of War Powers Resolutions to end the war in Iran six separate times – with bipartisan support for the effort steadily growing:

March 5, 2026 – vote fails 212 - 219, with two Republicans voting YEA

April 16, 2026 – vote fails 213 - 214, with four Republicans abstaining

May 14, 2026 – vote fails after 212 - 212 tie with three Republicans voting YEA

June 3, 2026 – vote PASSES 215 - 208, with four Republicans voting YEA

July 23, 2026 – vote PASSES 214 - 208, with seven Republicans abstaining

September 15, 2026 – vote PASSES 220 - 204, with seven Republicans voting YEA and eight abstaining

In May, amid reports that the Pentagon would seek $200B in supplemental funding for the war, Ryan introduced the No Funds for Iran War Act, which would prohibit the use of additional taxpayer funds for military action against Iran in the absence of an Authorization for the Use of Military Force (AUMF) or official declaration of war from Congress. Ryan introduced the legislation with the support of his fellow Democratic veterans in Congress, and it has continued to grow in support in the enduring months of the war.

In April, Ryan confronted Hegseth himself during a House Armed Services Committee hearing, pressing him on his failure to protect troops at Port Shuaiba. Following new reporting on the strike on Port Shuaiba, Ryan opened an investigation in August into how the Department of Defense failed to provide adequate medical care to service members injured and demanded answers about the Department's lack of preparation for a strike against Port Shuaiba.

In July, Ryan spoke on the House floor against handing Hegseth’s Pentagon a $1.5 trillion blank check through the FY27 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). He criticized colleagues for again refusing to consider his No Funds for Iran War Act, especially following the successful passage of a War Powers Resolution.

“It's personal to me. Having served twenty-seven months in combat in Iraq. Watching us double down on a losing strategy, year after year, while my friends and fellow soldiers – many of whose names are on this memorial bracelet I wear – fought and died. It's personal to the now eighteen families who lost their loved ones in this reckless war in Iran — sons, daughters, husbands, wives, somebody's whole world. It’s personal to the hundreds more wounded, many carrying injuries that will last their entire lives from this war,” Ryan said on the House floor.

Ryan’s full floor remarks can be viewed here.

Most recently, when the Trump administration tried to downplay the number of casualties in the war, Ryan again joined his Democratic veteran colleagues in demandingthe Administration accurately and transparently account for U.S. servicemembers killed and wounded in the Iran war.

Congressman Ryan is a U.S. Army veteran, served two combat tours in Iraq, and is the first West Point graduate to represent the Academy in the U.S. House of Representatives. Amid recent threats to veterans’ benefits, national security concerns, and rising threats worldwide, Congressman Ryan led his fellow veterans in Congress to create the Democratic Veterans Caucus. He sits on the House Armed Services Committee and has led extensive legislation to deliver relief for veterans, servicemembers, and military families.

Washington, D.C. – Today, Reps. John B. Larson (CT-01) and Joe Courtney (CT-02) applauded House passage of their Casualty Loss Dedication Restoration Act, which passed the House last night within the larger bill, H.R. 9500, by a vote of 408-17.

Larson and Courtney’s bill would allow homeowners impacted by crumbling foundations due to pyrrhotite to claim the casualty loss deduction for repair costs and allow homeowners to retroactively claim the deduction starting in 2021. In July, Rep. Larson successfully led passage of the bill through the Ways and Means Committee.

“More than a decade since the crumbling foundations crisis was first discovered in our region, up to 35,000 homes have been impacted,” said Larson. “Time and time again, families have had to foot the bill to repair their foundations—damaged through no fault of their own. I worked with my colleagues on the Ways and Means Committee to advance real tax relief, so homeowners can afford to make the repairs they need, and those who already replaced their foundations can be made whole. I want to thank my friend and colleague, Congressman Joe Courtney, for his tireless efforts and partnership to get this bill across the finish line with today’s strong, bipartisan vote in the House. I urge the Senate to act, so we can finally get Connecticut homeowners the support and certainty they deserve.”

“House passage of this bill to bring long overdue relief to Connecticut homeowners impacted by crumbling foundations is only possible because of Congressman John Larson’s work and leadership on the Ways and Means Committee,” said Courtney. “Thousands of homes in northcentral and eastern Connecticut have been plagued with crumbling concrete foundations caused by the mineral pyrrhotite, leaving families with exorbitant repair costs up to the hundreds of thousands of dollars through no fault of their own. By finally restoring the casualty loss deduction for all taxpayers after it was drastically restricted by President Trump’s 2017 tax law and allowing homeowners to amend prior-year tax returns for repairs to crumbling foundations caused by pyrrhotite made during calendar years 2021-2025, Congress can provide overdue relief to impacted homeowners. The Senate must now act swiftly to take up and pass this bill.”

As a senior Member of the Ways and Means Committee, Congressman Larson worked with Republican Ways and Means Committee Chair Jason Smith (MO-08), and the Democratic Ranking Member, Richard E. Neal (MA-01), to find a bipartisan path forward on tax relief for homeowners with crumbling foundations.

This legislation builds on the work of Rep. Larson and Rep. Courtney, who secured guidance from the IRS in 2017 that allowed homeowners to use the casualty loss deduction to help pay for foundation repairs. Once the provision was limited by the 2017 Republican Tax Law, the lawmakers secured a second ruling allowing homeowners to continue to use the deduction through 2021. Starting in 2021, that law left the thousands of Eastern and Central Connecticut homeowners impacted by crumbling foundations unable to claim a tax deduction for unreimbursed costs related to fixing their home. Larson and Courtney’s legislation will ensure no Connecticut homeowners are left out simply because of when the repairs were made.
title: Larson, Courtney Applaud House Passage of Their Bill to Restore Tax Relief for Homeowners with Crumbling Foundations

CHARLOTTE, N.C. – Bryan Tromon Green, 35, of Gastonia, N.C., was sentenced to 151 months in prison today followed by four years of supervised release for distributing fentanyl-laced pills and selling firearms in Gaston County, announced Russ Ferguson, U.S. Attorney for the Western District of North Carolina. Green’s co-conspirator, Jarvis Sentell Lynn, 38, also of Gastonia, was previously sentenced to 110 months in prison and three years of supervised release for trafficking fentanyl and cocaine.

“When repeat felons like this spread deadly drugs and illegal guns on our streets, we will take those cases federal to put an end to it,” said U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson

“The combination of drug dealing and illegal firearm possession is a recipe for violence and tragedy,” said ATF Special Agent in Charge Alicia Jones. “Taking back firearms from prohibited individuals and stopping the flow of drugs into our communities is a priority for ATF and all of our law enforcement partners.”

According to court documents, law enforcement determined that Green and Lynn, both multiple-time convicted felons, were selling drugs and firearms in Gaston County. Between March 2024 and April 2024, Green sold fentanyl pills multiple times to a confidential informant working with law enforcement. During the investigation, the confidential informant also purchased two firearms from Green: a Walther, Model PK380, .380 caliber semi-automatic pistol and an American Tactical Imports, Model Omni Hybrid, 5.56 caliber semi-automatic rifle.

Court documents show that, from March to May 2024, law enforcement also set up multiple controlled drug purchases with Lynn at his residence in Gastonia for pills pressed with fentanyl. During one of the controlled purchases, law enforcement also bought a Ruger, Model P89DC 9 mm semi-automatic pistol from Lynn. On May 16, 2024, law enforcement executed a search warrant at Lynn’s residence, seizing firearms, ammunition, and drugs. Specifically, law enforcement located and seized a Taurus, Model G3C, 9mm semi-automatic pistol; Point Blank body armor; a Smith & Wesson, Model SD9VE, 9mm semi-automatic pistol; an SKS style rifle; an extended rifle magazine containing 32 rounds of 7.62x39mm ammunition; a Hi-Point, Model C9, 9mm semiautomatic pistol; additional magazines and 9mm rounds of ammunition; plastic baggies used for drug distribution; digital scales; marijuana; and cocaine.

Green and Lynn both pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute and to possess with intent to distribute fentanyl and cocaine and distribution of fentanyl. They are in federal custody and will be transferred to the custody of the Federal Bureau of Prisons upon designation to a federal facility.

This investigation was led by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives and the Gaston County Police Department.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Nick J. Miller of the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Charlotte prosecuted the case.
title: Gastonia Distributor of Fentanyl-Laced Pills Sentenced to Over 12 Years in Prison

Murder Suspect on the Run for Three Years Captured in Slovenia
For immediate release
Millington, TN - Seth Walls, 23, was wanted on charges of Second-Degree Murder and Reckless Endangerment-Deadly Weapon was captured in Ljubljana, Slovenia.
On September 11, 2022, a 15-year-old-female was shot to death at a residence in in the 5000 block of Clear Creek Drive in Millington, Tennessee. After an investigation by the Millington Police Department, an arrest warrant was issued through Shelby County Criminal Court for Seth Walls, who was a Millington resident at the time, on charges of Second-Degree Murder and Reckless Endangerment-Deadly Weapon.
The case was adopted for a fugitive investigation by the U.S. Marshals Two Rivers Violent Fugitive Task Force in Memphis on September 25, 2023. Walls’ trail led out of state and eventually out of the country. Interpol was brought into the investigation to keep police agencies in other countries on the hunt for Walls.
On September 12, 2026, Walls was arrested in Ljubljana, Slovenia. Although he was using an assumed name, fingerprints provided by Interpol proved it was indeed Seth Walls.
Walls currently remains in custody in Slovenia. The Shelby County District Attorney’s Office and the Shelby County Sheriff’s Office will coordinate the extradition back to the United States.
“This fugitive investigation spanned three years and overseas to Europe, but the U.S. Marshals Service never stopped hunting Seth Walls,” said Tyreece Miller, U.S. Marshal for the Western District of Tennessee. “We are glad to utilize the skills of our Investigators and coordinate with local, federal, and international law enforcement partners to hold him accountable to the justice system and the victim’s family.”
“The arrest of Seth Walls in Slovenia is a powerful example of what can be accomplished when local, state, federal, and international law enforcement agencies work together, said Shelby County Sheriff Anthony Buckner. “I commend the U.S. Marshals Service and all our law enforcement partners for their determination and persistence. We will continue working with the District Attorney’s Office to bring Walls back to Shelby County so that he can face the charges against him and allow the judicial process to move forward.”
“I’m pleased the Marshals Service was able to find the defendant, even as far as Slovenia,” said DA Steve Mulroy. “It demonstrates that no matter where people are in the world the Marshals can find them. I also appreciate the cooperation of the FBI and other law enforcement agencies. Our office will work with the Sheriff’s Office to extradite him as soon as practicable, so the criminal justice process can proceed without delay.”
“The City of Millington extends its sincere appreciation to the U.S. Marshals Service, District Attorney’s Office, and all law enforcement personnel who have worked diligently on this case,” said Gary Graves, City of Millington Director of Public Safety. “Justice for Ms. Reedy has been a priority since the tragic day and we are glad that our law enforcement partners made it clear that Mr. Walls has nowhere on this Earth to run to.”
“The tragic murder of Haley Reedy has deeply affected her family, friends, and the whole Millington Community,” said Larry Dagen, City of Millington Mayor. “We recognize that no action can undo that loss, but we hope this significant development in the case provides an opportunity for justice to be done and brings the family, and our community, closer to healing.”
The Gulf Shores Alabama Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Millington Police Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation assisted in the investigation.
title: Murder Suspect on the Run for Three Years Captured in Slovenia | U.S. Marshals Service
