text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Congressman Steny H. Hoyer (MD-05) was featured in the University of Maryland's (UMD) Terp Magazine Fall 2026 edition. Click here to read the story or see below:

STENY HOYER YIELDS THE FLOOR

By John Tucker

September 4, 2026

Sipping a Beer at a Capitol Hill soirée in 1988, John Berry ’80 overheard a congressional staffer mention that a Virginia university was lobbying the National Archives to build a huge facility on its campus to house millions of its documents. The next morning Berry tipped off his boss, U.S. Rep. Steny H. Hoyer ’63, that the prized repository was in play.

Within days, Hoyer and University System of Maryland Chancellor John S. Toll were leading the archivist of the United States on a tour of UMD’s campus; a couple of weeks later, Hoyer added an earmark to an appropriations bill establishing UMD as the site of the eventual 1.8 million-square-foot building. A befuddled Virginia staffer who later ran into Berry said, “I’ve never been so thoroughly sideswiped. Hoyer outsmarted us.”

Hoyer recalls the coup jubilantly: “Now it’s probably the premier archival institution in the world,” he says. “We brought some fantastic researchers to the campus.”

It was a classic move by Hoyer, who will retire from a 45-year career in Congress when his term ends in January. The longest-serving member of either chamber to represent Maryland, Hoyer shaped the influential 5th District abutting Washington into a research powerhouse, helping pump billions of dollars into behemoths like NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, Patuxent River Naval Air Station and NOAA Center for Weather and Climate Prediction, many of them tightly aligned with the University of Maryland.

“Steny’s leadership resulted in the modern federal research presence in the state of Maryland,” says emeritus UMD trustee Tim Maloney, a former state delegate whose district overlapped with Hoyer’s. “He did it quietly and without recognition. He was just interested in seeing results.”

The No. 2 member of the Democratic caucus for two decades—second only to Rep. Nancy Pelosi, an ally and frequent sparring partner—Hoyer played the role of happy warrior and shrewd tactician, a consensus-building centrist who complemented her street-fighting progressivism. The 87-year-old has spent nearly his entire career in public office; Hoyer was elected in 1966 to the Maryland Senate and joined the U.S. House of Representatives in 1981.

"[Hoyer] is one of the most underrated giants of U.S. legislative history." John Berry '80 Former Staffer and Ambassador to Australia

Still popular—he won 72% of the vote in his district in the 2024 primary—Hoyer walks away as the only Marylander to serve as majority leader. A throwback to an era when members of both major parties respected each other, he helped steer the passage of bipartisan landmark legislation including the 1990 American with Disabilities Act and the 2002 Help Americas Vote Act in response to the contested 2000 presidential election, the most sweeping election reform since the Voting Rights Act.

“He is one of the most underrated giants of U.S. legislative history,” says Berry, who after working for Hoyer ran President Obama’s Office of Personnel Management and served as ambassador to Australia.

Following retirement, Hoyer will donate his official papers to UMD Libraries, a collection that contains everything from personal notes, speeches, photos, campaign materials and correspondences with constituents and colleagues.

“From the very beginning, the University of Maryland has been a big part of my life, and I’m very proud of it,” he says.

Born in New York, Hoyer moved to District Heights, Md., as a child and enrolled in UMD in 1957 (tuition: $178). After posting 1.7 and 1.0 GPAs his freshman year, he took a semester off, then reenrolled, still without direction.

One day that spring, he was set to leave campus when a Pontiac convertible cruised by, carrying the guest speaker to the annual convocation ceremony. Hoyer thought the car looked cool and decided to follow it.

The teenager sat in awe as the handsome young U.S. senator talked passionately about politics and implored graduates to serve their communities and country. Immediately drawn to public service, Hoyer now calls his walk to the field house to hear John F. Kennedy “my road to Damascus.”

He changed his major from business to government and politics and was elected student government vice president. After marrying his high school sweetheart and graduating with high honors, Hoyer enrolled in Georgetown law school and joined the campaign team of U.S. Rep. Daniel Brewster of Maryland; there, he met a young staffer from Baltimore named Nancy D’Alesandro, who the following year became Nancy Pelosi. After he was elected president of the Maryland Young Democrats, anointed by The Washington Post as “a man to watch” and remained on staff when Brewster became a U.S. senator, he made his first run for elected office, distinguishing himself in a crowded field vying for a state Senate seat with a platform on fair housing.

The newly drawn district had backed segregationist candidate George Wallace in the 1964 presidential election, but Hoyer focused on a concentration of Black constituents, knocking on doors till his knuckles hurt. “People saw a skinny white kid looking younger than my 26 years, and said, ‘What are you doing here?’” he recalls. He won Black voters’ support nearly 7-to-1 and claimed the seat by 300 votes. In Annapolis, he cast one of his first votes to end the ban on interracial marriage.

At 35, he became Maryland’s youngest-ever Senate president, championing a district growing increasingly Black, educated, affluent and attractive to federal government workers. In 1981 he won a special election to represent the U.S. House’s 5th District, earning the nickname Boy Wonder.

“There was a certain way Steny Hoyer’s heels click-clicked along the marble halls of the State House that set him apart from the others. He had the sharpest, most urgent click-click in Annapolis,” the Post wrote upon his departure from the legislature.

Among his new constituents was Yvette Lewis, a Prince George’s County music teacher who dreamed of singing professionally—if only she could get her foot in the door at the Kennedy Center. Her husband suggested she call her congressman; maybe she could speak with a staffer. With surprising ease, she secured a meeting with Hoyer. She left with a smile and no expectations, but two weeks later received a letter from the Kennedy Center offering an interview.

Lewis landed a Kennedy Center teaching job, then a Washington Opera audition, then a resident understudy position. Following the contentious 2000 presidential election, she became politically active and ultimately served as chair of the Maryland Democratic Party for eight years. “Steny Hoyer changed my life,” she says.

Hoyer didn’t remember their original meeting when they first bumped into each other in political circles years later, but that didn’t surprise her.

“I’m not unique,” says Lewis, now a close friend who sits on the University System of Maryland Board of Regents. “I’m one of a million Hoyer stories.”

Hoyer gradually built his influence in Congress, chairing the Helsinki Commission on U.S.-European security, earning a seat on the powerful House Appropriations Committee and traveling to Darfur and South Sudan to raise awareness of genocide. He became Pelosi’s chief lieutenant in 2003 and House majority leader in 2007, charged with scheduling floor business and mobilizing the party vote on important legislation.

With increased clout, he directed millions of dollars into UMD programs through federal agency appropriations. A savvy analyst, he identified potential research partnerships, joint faculty appointments and student pipelines connecting UMD to the government, then brokered behind-the-scenes deals.

“He might tell his colleagues in the House, ‘Hey, the engineering school’s developing a remote sensing program that would be great for NASA Goddard,’” says Brian Darmody, chief strategy officer for the Association of University Research Parks. Formerly UMD’s assistant vice president for research and economic development, he worked closely with Hoyer in the 2000s to establish M Square, a public-private research hub that has since grown into UMD’s Discovery District Maryland.

Hoyer also secured funds from the Department of Defense for a UMD center now known as the Applied Research Lab for Intelligence and Security; from the Department of Agriculture for the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center, where more than two dozen UMD faculty work; and from the Food and Drug Administration for its Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition, which has a research partnership with UMD in College Park. On campus, Hoyer also helped net construction money for the Physical Sciences Complex and The Clarice Smith Performing Arts Center.

Meanwhile, he continued preaching in support of civil rights. In 2010, when a bill to end the “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell” policy banning gay Americans from serving openly in the military died in committee, Hoyer sidestepped the blockade by orchestrating a second Senate vote at the eleventh hour of the session, a “political miracle,” says Berry, his former staffer.

Hoyer was the first person whom Berry came out to as gay, after his parents. When Berry’s partner died of AIDS, Hoyer pulled over on Route 50 and listened to him weep on the phone for 30 minutes.

“He’s not only the best boss I’ve ever had, but a mentor, a second father, a true saint,” says Berry.

Hoyer looks younger han his 87 years, and he knows it. “God’s been good,” he says, after practically bounding into his office on the top floor of the Longworth building in crisp shirtsleeves and a yellow tie. Mentally sharp, though unsure whether he could deliver at 89, he is retiring somewhat reluctantly. Pelosi, his longtime colleague, is also stepping down at age 86.

One corner of Hoyer’s office is dedicated to the late Rep. John Lewis, one of his closest friends in Congress, with whom he marched 15 times across the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Ala., to make good trouble. In an opposite corner is the flag of Denmark (the self-described “proud Dane” in 2009 was honored as a Knight of the Order of the Dannebrog).

After retirement, he’ll remain active in Democratic politics and spend more time in his St. Mary’s County home. A rabid UMD football and basketball fan, he intends to keep shouting at nearly every home game alongside his wife, Elaine Kamarck, a director at a public policy nonprofit whom he married in 2023. (Hoyer’s first wife, the educator Judy Pickett Hoyer, died in 1997, leading Hoyer to create early-childhood programs across Maryland in her name.)

He’ll leave the House having shaped the careers of hundreds of staffers, including Jazz Lewis ’11, MPP ’14, who met Hoyer as a graduate student intending to become a community organizer. Instead, he agreed to lead his reelection campaign the day after commencement.

“His approach to public service was kindness, thoughtfulness and always following up. Every function was super long because he listened to everyone—it didn’t matter if they were a mechanic or someone’s granny,” says Lewis, who became Hoyer’s senior policy adviser and is now UMD’s director of state government relations.

Hoyer’s seat will almost certainly be inherited by another recent campaign manager, 32-year-old state Del. Adrian Boafo, who in June won the Democratic primary.

Ever congenial, the lion of the House laments that American politics has devolved into pettiness and divisiveness over the last decade. Still, he’s an optimist, easily quoting from Kennedy’s 1961 inaugural address: “The torch has been passed to a new generation of Americans ... unwilling to witness or permit the slow undoing of those human rights to which this nation has always been committed.”

Twelve presidential administrations later, in an emotional January speech on the House floor to announce his retirement, Hoyer passed his own torch, urging his colleagues to examine their conscience and renew their courage: “We must remember that we are not great or unique because we say we’re great, but because we are just, generous and fair.”

"I believe in democracy. I believe that over time, people mostly do the right thing." Steny Hoyer '63

text:
Interview

Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

September 8, 2026

Via Teleconference

September 9, 2026

(Via translation.)

QUESTION: Well, it is a tremendous honor to have with us here at RCN and NTN24 the United States Secretary of State, Marco Rubio. Secretary, thank you for being here with us.

SECRETARY RUBIO: No, thanks. It’s a great honor to be with you as well.

QUESTION: They are also watching us in Miami and throughout Latin America thanks to NTN24. As you know, we are networks that have followed your work closely since you were a senator and now as Secretary of State. And now you come to a country like Colombia, one that is not unfamiliar to you, because it must be said that you have defended democracy in our country, Colombia. Additionally, if you’ll allow me a personal question, your wife also has very deep roots in this country. What is your personal connection to Colombia?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, my wife—her mother was born in [inaudible], stayed in [inaudible], and then moved to Bogotá. She still has relatives here. And I live in Miami, and I don’t know if you know this, but there are a lot of Colombians in Miami.

QUESTION: Lots of them.

SECRETARY RUBIO: And that’s why I wanted to mention it. And in Broward as well. But I have always followed Colombia very closely for two reasons. The personal connection is always important, and we follow everything that happens in the country very closely because of that relationship, but also because of the relationship between our two countries. You have to understand that for more than 20 years, throughout my entire time in the Senate, for example, the most important partner we had in South America was Colombia, the most consistent one. There were changes of government in different places, but when it came to economic and security matters, the most important partner the United States had was Colombia. That was broken over the last four years. Unfortunately, although many relationships still existed at the military and security levels and so forth, we went through a period that, I would say, was not natural in our relationship. It was somewhat damaged, unfortunately. But now we are entering a new stage, and I believe we are quickly going to recover what we had—and not simply recover what we had. We are going to be able to expand it even further, because you have a president here who has tremendous enthusiasm, a lot of energy, a lot of vision, and who is willing to take risks, but who is also responsible and knows the American system well. He understands well how our system works. That is also going to help him greatly in building that connection.

QUESTION: In fact, I remember you saying, “The best days are yet to come for Colombia,” after your meeting with Abelardo de la Espriella, and I imagine you still feel the same way. But for that to happen, we need cooperation, especially on an issue that I know has long been a concern for both you and the President: security. How do you view the security situation in Colombia?

SECRETARY RUBIO: I have said it, and I will continue to say it. The most important responsibility of any government, at any level—municipal, departmental, state, as we say in the United States, or at the federal or national level—is security. It is the most important thing the government does: security. The security of a country, the security of a community, the security, the security of its people, and that is the most important thing. And to a certain extent, I think that was somewhat neglected in the thinking of the previous government over the last three or four years. You have a president who was very clearly elected, who made it very clear during his campaign and has made it clear now as president that his number one priority is to restore stability and security for the Colombian people, and we are going to help in every way possible. On top of that foundation of security comes prosperity. Prosperity is impossible without security. It is impossible to invest in a country that is unsafe. It is impossible to invest in a country that is dominated by cartels or criminal gangs. In many cases, these are not just Colombian criminal gangs; they are transnational, operating in Ecuador, Mexico, and other countries in the region. So, for us, security is fundamental. It is the most fundamental thing a government does, and these threats affect us as well, so we are going to help in every way possible. But it is not just about security; it is about security and prosperity. The two go together.

QUESTION: Look, Secretary, we are being attacked with drones by illegal armed groups, and in that regard, support with technology and upgrading equipment that is already obsolete in Colombia is very important. But there is another issue that is also of great concern, and that is the attacks coming from the other side of the border. You know that Venezuela has granted impunity to many of those criminals. What can the United States do on both fronts? Technological and Venezuela. And the criminals?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Let’s talk first about the situation in Venezuela. We have the ELN and the president of the FARC operating openly and with impunity from Venezuelan territory. This has been going on for more than 10, 15 years. That has to be resolved. We have made that clear to the interim authorities in Venezuela, and I think that is going to be key to improving relations between the two countries. It is impossible for relations to truly improve while that issue remains as it is. No country can allow criminal gangs and terrorists to operate with impunity on the other side of its border, attack within its national territory, and then return under the protection of another country’s borders. That cannot be allowed, and we are going to help with that. And we have already spoken with the Venezuelan authorities, including on the issue of drones. The technology is a global threat. This is a global threat because there is a lot of military equipment that requires a government with millions of dollars in order to acquire it. But in the case of these drones, that really is not necessary. Even criminal gangs can possess them and use them to attack and threaten a state. So, one of the things that is needed worldwide, not just in Colombia, is to establish new, modern defenses against this new threat, specifically drones that use fiber optics, which pose an enormous danger because at this time there is no conventional defense against them. So we have already had discussions about that.

QUESTION: And is the United States willing to help Colombia?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Yes, but we are not only willing to help Colombia; we also need it for our own resources. So, both countries have an interest in developing the new technology necessary to prevent this type of attack and defend against it.

QUESTION: Secretary, during the previous administration of President Gustavo Petro, the United States decertified us in the fight against drugs. How close are we to, or how far are we from, being certified again?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, remember that the certification announced this year has to do with the actions that took place last year. We have a completely different view when it comes to the new president and the new administration, this team. So I expect that if they continue to follow through and continue doing what they say they are going to do and what they have already done—I mean, in the last month we have seen more concrete action against these criminal groups than we possibly saw in four years. So I think that if they continue on that path, there is no doubt that the certification will change, as it has in the past.

QUESTION: How soon or how far away is that?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, that’s done on an annual basis. It’s possible that it can be done earlier because there’s a waiver process to be able to do it sooner.

QUESTION: Are you going to help us in that, I imagine?

SECRETARY RUBIO: I, I, what I—I’m going to do everything possible to help Colombia. And obviously, if the new government continues as it already is, it’s not that they’re making promises; they’re already doing it, and they have begun acting against that. I expect that to change.

QUESTION: Secretary, there is another issue that is also of great concern to small, large, and medium-sized businesses, and I’m sure it has come up in the conversations you have had over the past month and in the one you had today in Barranquilla. The issue of tariffs on certain products is affecting us. Uh, they are asking for a temporary suspension of some of those tariffs. Are you leaving us with that good news, or are we not there yet?

SECRETARY RUBIO: The tariffs, first of all, apply to everyone. They are not specifically directed at Colombia. This is worldwide. The Supreme Court and its ruling against the President’s policy required a change in strategy and the use of a new process, Section 302, which is a U.S. domestic process that is very legal, very, very technical. But the President wants to change that. The way this issue can be resolved is through a bilateral agreement between the two countries, and negotiations on that are underway. I believe there have been two rounds of negotiations, they have progressed very well, and I hope that very soon the issue can be resolved through that agreement between the two countries. And for President Trump, it is a priority. He has said so. He wants to follow through and bring this to a conclusion. He wants to reach a bilateral agreement that eliminates the problem we currently have with the tariffs.

QUESTION: Well, that’s good. Hopefully that will be the case. Secretary, I know you are very diplomatic, and you are going to tell me that you cannot say much about the OFAC list and former officials such as President Petro, Armando Benedetti, and others. But tell me, are there any ongoing investigations by the United States into that?

SECRETARY RUBIO: It’s not that I’m being diplomatic; I cannot offer opinions or comment on investigations, whether active or not. I cannot comment on that. What I can tell you is that with all these sanctions, in our system there is no sanction that is imposed without evidence, and the evidence is not going to be ignored. If there is evidence that someone has committed a crime, is committing a crime, or has caused harm, that will be pursued. That is not up to me.

QUESTION: Are there any active investigations underway?

SECRETARY RUBIO: I can’t comment on that because investigations are not under my purview. They are handled by the Department of Justice. So, I cannot comment on whether there are or are not. What I can tell you is that no one ends up on the, on the OFAC list because someone made something up. To be placed on the OFAC list, there have to be facts, there has to be evidence, there have to be concrete things that justify that decision.

QUESTION: In the case of these officials.

SECRETARY RUBIO: And there may possibly be others who are placed on that list at some point, if there is evidence against them as well.

QUESTION: Look, on that note, Gustavo Petro used to say that you had misinformed President Donald Trump. Gustavo Petro is no longer in Colombia; he is no longer the president of Colombia. What does Marco Rubio think of Gustavo Petro?

SECRETARY RUBIO: I think he is no longer president, and we are going to deal with the president you have. He is someone I have known for several years, since before he entered politics. I joked earlier that he went crazy and got into politics. But he is someone who was elected by the people of this country and someone we are going to work with.

QUESTION: Just so you know, President Abelardo responded, “And you’re next.”

SECRETARY RUBIO: Something like that, I think. I didn’t quite understand it; I didn’t see it very clearly, but he—but I had already been in politics for many years. He wasn’t a politician; he had never been a politician. He was interested in politics, but he wasn’t a politician. I knew him as a local businessman in Miami, and then he wanted to contribute to his country, he wanted to help his country. He ran for president when no one thought he was going to win, and he won. And now he is president, and he is the one we are going to deal with. I’m not going to dwell on the past.

QUESTION: Look, I know time is short. We’re wrapping up now, Secretary, I promise. But let me ask you about a country that is, close to you, which is Cuba, and also about Nicaragua. What can the United States, and the world, do to finally bring those dictatorships to an end?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, as in every country, first, the primary responsibility for changing a system lies with the people of those countries. That is always the case. Obviously, we do not support what is happening, or what they are doing, in Nicaragua, and we have imposed sanctions against individuals, people who are contributing to the situation that currently exists in Nicaragua. When it comes to Cuba, what we are not going to continue allowing is for a military company called GAESA to keep stealing Cuba’s money, and that is why we have imposed the strongest sanctions in the history of our relationship with Cuba. Tragically, the Cuban people are suffering, but they are not suffering because of us. They are suffering for two reasons. First, because the individuals in charge of that regime are following an economic model that does not work and has never worked. But now it does not work because they have become accustomed, for more than 60 years, to living off assistance from abroad. First, it was the Soviet Union, then it was Hugo Chávez, and when the free oil they were stealing from Venezuela ran out, they were left without oil. That is not our fault. That is their fault for not having a functioning market. And second, because some—many of the leaders in Cuba who are currently part of that regime are incompetent. They do not know how to manage the economy, and they are the ones who have directly contributed to the suffering of the Cuban people. But what we are not going to allow is for them to continue evading sanctions in order to benefit themselves at the expense of the Cuban people.

QUESTION: And what do you mean by not allowing it? Carrying out an operation like the one in Venezuela?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Not allowing it—well, for example, we are already doing that. We have shut down bank accounts. Many, many foreign companies have left Cuba because of these sanctions, and they have left because those companies were partners, they had entered into business dealings with these elements of the regime, and they were enriching themselves.

QUESTION: But could tougher measures be coming, Secretary?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I’m not going to speculate about what those measures might be, but we always have the right to operate and take action to protect the national security of the United States. I’m not going to comment specifically on exactly what can be done, but we have an obligation to protect the national security of the United States if a threat arises in Cuba, Venezuela, or anywhere else in the world.

QUESTION: Look, one thing: the possibility of having U.S. military bases in Colombia, yes or no?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Anything is possible. Obviously, this has to come through—first, we have to be invited, because this is a sovereign country, and the decision has to be made by the Venezuelan people through—sorry, by the Colombian people, through their elected officials. If they officially make that request to us, then it will be considered to see what is possible. At the end of the day, that decision is up to the President, through the U.S. Department of Defense, the Department of War. But what I can tell you, without a doubt, is that the security relationship between the United States and Colombia is not going to be the same as before; it is going to be better.

QUESTION: Look, I’ll wrap up, but as we say here in Colombia, President Abelardo de la Espriella gave me the task to ask you about your political future. The 2028 elections. Am I interviewing one of the strongest candidates for 2028?

SECRETARY RUBIO: But I’m not a candidate for anything right now, and I’m 100% focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs. I have my job as Secretary of State, and I also work as the President’s National Security Advisor, so I have plenty of work right now.

QUESTION: But is the dream of becoming President of the United States there?

SECRETARY RUBIO: Well, I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time. I’m 100% focused on my jobs.

QUESTION: Secretary, and speaking of that job, we want to thank you, on behalf of all Colombians, for what you have done for this country and for its democracy. And please, continue to keep in mind cooperation based on equality, trust, and respect between the United States and Colombia. Thank you, Marco Rubio.

SECRETARY RUBIO: Thank you very much.

LOS ANGELES – An Inglewood woman has been arrested on a 15-count federal grand jury indictment charging her with defrauding venture capital funds out of more than $13 million by lying about her credentials and her now-defunct tax compliance startup company’s revenue, then using investors’ money to purchase a home, a Tesla, and pay for her wedding in the Caribbean, the Justice Department announced today.

Shiloh Luckey, 42, a.k.a. “Shiloh Johnson,” was arrested on Sunday in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, before she attempted to board a cruise ship for a vacation. Luckey was released on bond in the Southern District of Florida and is expected to appear in United States District Court in downtown Los Angeles in the coming weeks.

Luckey is charged with nine counts of securities fraud, three counts of wire fraud, one count of bank fraud, and two counts of money laundering.

According to the indictment returned on September 1, Luckey founded the Los Angeles-based ComplYant App Inc. in 2019 and presented it as a tax compliance startup company that offered services to small businesses to help them navigate complex tax regulations in exchange for a monthly subscription fee. Luckey was ComplYant’s CEO and exerted managerial control over the company.

From September 2020 to September 2023, Luckey defrauded investors by promoting ComplYant as having existing customers and a significant recurring revenue stream. As part of the alleged scheme, Luckey persuaded victims to invest in the company by presenting them with pitch decks, investor materials, and updates that falsely inflated ComplYant’s revenue, customer base, subscriptions, and cash reserve balances.

Luckey also induced victims to invest by lying to them and representing that she was a licensed certified public accountant (CPA) with deep expertise in tax management, accounting, and compliance, when, in fact, she has never been a licensed CPA.

Relying on these false statements, pretenses, and misrepresentations, victims invested millions of dollars into ComplYant under the belief it was a promising start-up based on Luckey’s representations.

Luckey then used a portion of these funds to pay for personal expenses, including the purchase of her residence, the purchase of a Tesla automobile, and to pay her wedding on the Caribbean island of Anguilla.

By September 2023, ComplYant experienced severe liquidity issues and ceased operations, causing the investors to lose their investments.

In total, Luckey fraudulently obtained at least $13.3 million from her victims, with the victims losing their entire investments.

The indictment further alleges that, in September and October of 2022, Luckey engaged in a check kiting scheme to purchase her Inglewood home by intentionally writing a bad $1.5 million check from a ComplYant account with insufficient funds, depositing it into another ComplYant account at a different bank, and wiring the money to buy her home before the first bank realized the check was worthless.

Luckey then paid off the negative balance caused by her check kiting scheme by repaying the negative bank account balance with fresh proceeds from her securities fraud.

An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

If convicted of all charges, Luckey would face a statutory maximum sentence of 30 years in federal prison on the bank fraud count, up to 20 years in federal prison for each securities fraud and wire fraud count, and a statutory maximum sentence of 10 years in federal prison for each money laundering count.

The FBI is investigating this matter.

Assistant United States Attorney Andrew M. Roach of the Major Frauds Section is prosecuting this case.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – On September 9, 2026, U.S. Representative Gabe Vasquez (NM-02) announced that his office has returned more than $7.6 million to constituents in New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District through casework services, just over a month since announcing the $6 million milestone. Rep. Vasquez’s casework team helps constituents cut past red tape and resolve issues with federal agencies, including the IRS, Social Security Administration, Department of Veterans Affairs, and more.

“I’m incredibly proud of this milestone for our office and most importantly, for the $7.6 million we’ve returned to our constituents,” said Vasquez. “My staff and I remain laser-focused on helping every constituent that walks through our door navigate the excessive red tape in federal agencies, resolve their issues, and get justice and the money they are owed. Our work for New Mexicans continues.”

“I retired from the military on 31-Dec-25. Working with DFAS and other Military agencies, I hadn’t received retirement payment or proper deductions for 8 months. I contacted Gabe Vasquez’s office and they spoke with DFAS and the Air Force on my behalf. Gabe Vasquez’s office had everything corrected within 10 business days of them starting their inquiry on my behalf,” said Jacob of Holloman AFB.

“I contacted Congressman Vasquez for help regarding the delay I was experiencing with the Social Security Administration in converting my spousal benefits to survivor benefits after my husband's death. I was quite frustrated for several months after I had made repeated calls to SSA to find out when they would make this adjustment. In just a week after contacting Congressman Vasquez I was delighted to receive my retroactive payments and notice that I would from now on receive my new monthly survivor benefits,” said Sara of Albuquerque.

“My 2025 tax return was set aside and not processed for an administrative reason, holding up my refund. [Vasquez’s Office] responded quickly to my request for help and was able to resolve the issue holding up the processing of my return and just as quickly I received my refund. Good government in action. I am deeply appreciative,” said Michael of Truth or Consequences.

Vasquez’s office also frequently holds Mobile Office Hours to assist constituents in rural communities and cities throughout New Mexico – from Belen, to Anthony, to Deming, you can find the office available to help. For more information on how to attend mobile office hours or visit the office for assistance, you can follow Rep. Vasquez on instagram and facebook.

text:
FSIS Updates for Small Plants - September 9, 2026
Information for small and very small establishments
Executive Orders Direct FSIS to Expand State Inspection Programs and Support Small Processors
On September 4, President Donald J. Trump signed two Executive Orders supporting America’s ranchers. U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins also announced additional actions under the department’s Ranchers First Initiative. These actions are geared at rebuilding the American cattle herd and strengthening our domestic beef supply, while upholding the highest standards of food safety.
View the executive orders:
- Supporting American Ranchers
- Promoting Fair Competition in Livestock Markets and Expanding Market Access for American Meat Producers
These actions build on the Small Processors Action Plan and the Ranchers First Initiative to keep processing capacity and jobs in the communities where livestock is raised.
USDA Launches Program to Strengthen Independent Beef Processors and Support Ranchers
As announced in the August 7 Constituent Update, the USDA is accepting applications for the Strengthening Processing for U.S. Ranchers (SPUR) program.
The Farm Service Agency (FSA) is administering SPUR at the national office level under the Commodity Credit Corporation Charter Act, using FSIS data to identify eligible establishments and payment amounts. Beef processing establishments can apply if they are operating at the time of application and inspected federally by FSIS, through the Talmadge-Aiken Cooperative Inspection Program, or through the Cooperative Interstate Shipment (CIS) Program. University- and state-owned entities, entities with a foreign primary shareholder, and the four largest beef processing entities are not eligible.
As outlined in the August 14 Constituent Update, payments are based on 2025 processing throughput at a rate of $53.05 per head and will be issued in two rounds. All eligible establishments that apply and have slaughtered 50 percent of the 2025 numbers will receive a first payment of 50 percent of their eligible amount. The remaining 50 percent will be issued once the establishment processes 60 percent of its 2025 throughput between January 1 and December 31, 2026. FSIS will notify FSA when an establishment reaches that threshold, so no additional application or action is needed to receive the second payment.
SPUR funding comes with a payback condition. Establishments that cease business operations as beef processors or sell their establishment within two years of receiving funds may be required to return the money.
Potentially eligible establishments will receive partially pre-filled applications to the email address on file with FSIS. The application deadline has been extended to Sept. 30. To apply, complete and sign the application and email it to spurapplications@usda.gov by this date. Establishments that do not already have a Unique Entity ID should obtain one immediately from SAM.gov. SPUR payments are considered taxable income.
Reminders and Updates:
- SPUR eligibility is limited to active beef slaughter facilities under federal inspection, including establishments under the Talmadge-Aiken Cooperative Inspection Program as well as those under the CIS Program.
- SPUR applications are being sent directly to the primary contact on the FSIS Public Health Information System (PHIS) listserv.
- Establishments that first became operational in or after February 2025 or during 2026 may be eligible for proration. Eligible establishments will receive a new application no later than Friday, September 11.
- Assuming there are no issues with the application, payments are expected to be issued within 30 days of receipt, using the bank account information you have on file with SAM.gov.
- To avoid processing delays, please ensure that your SAM.gov registration exactly matches the establishment name on file with FSIS.
- As a reminder, your first payment will be 50 percent of the payment rate multiplied by your eligible head. Once your 2026 slaughter number reaches 60 percent of the eligible head listed on your application, FSIS will notify FSA to issue your second payment.
- For more details, view the August 11 webinar recording.
If you have questions about SPUR, please email SPUR@usda.gov. If you have received your application and have questions regarding the application itself, please email SPURapplications@usda.gov. To learn more, please visit https://fsa.usda.gov/spur.
FSIS Extends Overtime and Holiday Inspection Fee Reductions
As part of its ongoing commitment to support small and very small establishments, FSIS is extending temporary overtime and holiday inspection fee reductions for eligible small and very small establishments to fiscal year 2027, until available funds are expended. Eligible small establishments receive a 30 percent reduction, and eligible very small establishments receive a 75 percent reduction. Details are in the Federal Register notice.
Overtime use often looks different for smaller operators than it does for larger establishments. You may need inspection outside regular hours only periodically, to meet seasonal demand, cover staffing gaps, or keep up with a production schedule. The reduction applies to that occasional use as well.
To apply, complete FSIS Form 5200-16, Overtime/Holiday Rate Reduction Form, and submit it to the frontline supervisor assigned to your establishment or email it to your District Office, "Attention Grant Curator." Qualifying establishments receive a partial refund for overtime and holiday fees paid since October 5, 2025, as a lump sum or as a credit toward future fees. FSIS processes complete submissions in the order received while funds remain, so submit as soon as possible.
If you have questions about how the fee reduction applies to your operation, contact your District Office or submit a question through askFSIS.
FSIS Joins Flower Hill Institute Roundtable on Becoming USDA or CIS Inspected
On August 12, FSIS Deputy Administrator for Field Operations Robert Bane joined the Flower Hill Institute, a Meat and Poultry Processing Technical Assistance provider, for an online roundtable, “Passing Inspection: What it Takes to Be USDA or CIS Inspected.” The session topic came directly from participant feedback following previous Flower Hill roundtables and drew small and very small meat and poultry processors from across the country, including operators exploring federal inspection for the first time.
Bane was joined by two processors who recently completed the journey themselves: Danielle Carrillo of Clark’s Custom Meat Company in St. Joseph, Mo., which operates under the CIS Program, and Mark Siderius, chairman of Glacier Processing Cooperative in Columbia Falls, Mont., a producer-owned cooperative that transitioned its plant to full federal inspection. The panel walked through what happens after an application for inspection is submitted, common pitfalls that slow applications down, and how to approach noncompliance records constructively. Bane also covered what changed under the Small Processors Action Plan, and the resources available at every step, from District Office Grant Curators to the Small Plant Help Desk and the Applying for USDA FSIS Inspection guideline.
A recording of the roundtable is available on the Flower Hill Institute’s YouTube channel. If you are considering federal or CIS inspection and have questions, reach out through askFSIS or contact the Small Plant Help Desk by emailing InfoSource@usda.gov or calling 1-877-FSIS-HELP (1-877-374-7435).
Additional Resources:
- Applying for USDA FSIS Inspection guideline (FSIS-GD-2025-0005), on the FSIS website under FSIS Guidelines.
- Apply for Grant of Inspection webpage, which includes Form 5200-2, sample applications, and the full resource list.
- Small Plant Help Desk: 1-877-FSIS-HELP (1-877-374-7435), webform, or InfoSource@usda.gov
- askFSIS Q&A Portal for technical and regulatory questions.
- HACCP guidance webpage, the Guidebook for the Preparation of HACCP Plans, and university-affiliated State HACCP Coordinators who provide free one-on-one HACCP assistance.
- OFO directory with District Office Grant Curators, who walk applicants through the process directly.
- For tribal producers and Tribal Nation operations: the USDA Office of Tribal Relations: 202-205-2249 or Tribal.Relations@usda.gov.
- FSIS newsletters: the weekly Constituent Update and the monthly FSIS Updates for Small Plants newsletter. Subscribe at the FSIS website or by emailing FSIS@usda.gov.
- Small Processors Action Plan information.
FSIS Announces Leadership Changes
FSIS is announcing leadership changes that continue positioning the agency to effectively deliver on its food safety mission and support its strategic framework of strong people, smart systems and safe food.
Mr. Jeremy “Todd” Reed has been named deputy administrator for Science and Policy in the Office of the Administrator (OA). Reed brings decades of experience and expertise to this position and has served in several leadership positions within FSIS. Mr. Reed has been serving as FSIS’ chief operating officer since 2018.
Dr. Gabrial Eddings has been named assistant administrator for the Office of Public Health Science (OPHS). Dr. Eddings has served in several leadership positions within FSIS, most recently served as acting executive associate for regulatory operations within FSIS’ Office of Field Operations.
Dr. Glenn Tillman has been named deputy assistant administrator for OPHS. Dr. Tillman has over 25 years of experience with FSIS serving in multiple roles, within OPHS, including a branch chief for the Microbiology Characterization Branch.
Additional leadership changes were made in OA, OPHS and the Office of Public Affairs and Training (OPAT). Ms. Karen Hunter will be acting as chief operating officer in OA. Within OPHS, Ms. Kimberly Nguyen will serve as acting executive associate for laboratory services. Ms. Atiya Khan will be acting as assistant administrator of OPAT.
You can find these updates and information about FSIS leadership on the FSIS website.
FSIS to Host Webinar on the Modernized PHIS Domestic Inspection for Industry
FSIS invites industry stakeholders to a webinar to demonstrate the changes to Noncompliance Records, Appeals, and Memoranda of Interview in PHIS' modernized domestic inspection module. Additional Regulatory and Program Updates
The continued changes within FSIS are well-thought-out and designed to help our small and very small processors succeed. We have made strides to streamline inspection, improve available resources, enhanced metals and residue testing, and more. Read on to learn how FSIS is making strides while keeping our valuable smaller processor’s needs in mind.
Policy
An updated list of substances that may be used in the production of meat, poultry, and egg products is available in FSIS Directive 7120.1, Revision 62, issued on Aug. 20.
The comment period for the updated Food Safety Guideline for egg products closed on July 6. Comment reviews are underway for this guideline and on the advanced notice of proposed rulemaking on establishment size definitions, NPIS Line Speed and NSIS Line Speed proposals. We value your perspectives on these rulemaking efforts.
Sampling & Testing
FSIS announced an expansion of monitoring for chemical residues associated with veterinary drugs used to treat and prevent New World Screwworm in livestock species. Screening will be expanded for specific analytes from newly approved or authorized drugs on ovine, caprine, and porcine muscle and kidney. This testing builds on extended testing on bovine muscle and kidney announced on July 17. The updated methods will be posted to the Chemistry Laboratory Guidebook page of the FSIS website no later than September 1, 2026. Please direct questions regarding specific elements of any method to the USDA website via askFSIS.
Exports
Beginning September 3, the European Union (EU) will only accept products of animal origin from countries that meet Article 118 of Regulation (EU) 2019/6. FSIS has revised the EU Export Library page with the updated FSIS Letterhead Certificates for commercial shipments of beef, pork, poultry, and egg products exported for entry into the EU. Exporters must begin using these updated certificates, effective immediately. A transition period will be in place from August 21 through September 3. During this time, the EU will continue to accept previous versions of export certificates, provided they were certified by an FSIS veterinarian on or before September 3, 2026. Any certificates for commercial beef, pork, poultry, or egg products certified after that date must use the updated version.
On August 14, Morocco began accepting pork casings products from U.S. establishments. Any establishment interested in exporting pork casings products to Morocco must submit FSIS Form 9080-3 application through PHIS.
FSIS hosted a webinar on the new modernized PHIS export 9060 process on July 16. The session walked exporters and trade groups through the updated export application, which was made available in the PHIS Industry Test Environment (ITE) on July 27. The new process will start in September 2026, and you are all encouraged to explore PHIS ITE to ensure you’re familiar. An online demo from the webinar has also been made available to help refresh your memory and guide you through the new export application. FSIS will make additional resources available, including updated PHIS help tutorials and user guides, announced through the usual channels. For questions about the PHIS modernization changes, email PHISTechnicalQA@usda.gov.

LINCOLNSHIRE, IL – Today, Congressman Brad Schneider (IL-10) along with Congressman Craig Goldman (TX-12), Co-Chairs of the Abraham Accords Caucus, led a bipartisan group of colleagues to urge Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent to continue their efforts to prevent Hamas and other Iranian-backed groups from exploiting economic instability in the West Bank.

“The United States must confront and degrade terrorist organizations like Hamas and other Iran-backed actors that threaten U.S. interests and our allies, but we must not unnecessarily destabilize the West Bank in the process,” said Schneider. “As a Co-Chair of the Abraham Accords Caucus, I am committed to advancing efforts that build lasting peace and security for Israelis, Palestinians, and all the countries across the Middle East. A functioning Palestinian economy promotes greater stability and increased possibility for progress towards peace. The United States must work with Israel and the Palestinian Authority to advance reforms that keep clearance revenues flowing, disrupt terror financing, and preserve financial stability. I will continue working with colleagues across the aisle to put peace, stability, and security first, so that Israeli and Palestinian children can build prosperous futures.”

“Supporting Israel’s security and defeating terrorist groups is central to America’s foreign policy,” said Goldman. “Economic instability in the West Bank risks creating a vacuum that Hamas and other Iranian-backed terrorist organizations could exploit, further threatening Israel’s security and undermining regional peace and integration. Alongside Rep. Schneider, I’m urging Secretary Rubio and Secretary Bessent to continue policies that promote regional stability while ensuring strict accountability and preventing financial channels from illicitly supporting terrorism.”

“We recognize Israel’s legitimate security concerns since October 7, and we are not asking for Israel to relax vigilance against terror financing,” the members wrote. “However, continued withholding of billions in clearance revenues risks accelerating the West Bank’s fiscal collapse – an outcome that would serve the interests of extremist and Iran-backed groups, not Israel, nor the United States. We therefore urge you to work with Israel and the Palestinian Authority on practical, security conscious mechanisms that keep clearance revenues flowing to legitimate Palestinian institutions while ensuring none are diverted to terror financing.”

“We share the United States’ long-held position that the Palestinian Authority must implement meaningful reforms,” the members continued. “Real and sustainable reform, however, cannot succeed if the Palestinian institutions expected to carry it out are deprived of the revenues and financial infrastructure necessary to function. Despite its significant shortcomings and flaws, the Palestinian Authority remains the only current viable governing alternative to Hamas and thus must play an essential role in promoting regional stability and security. A fiscal collapse of the Palestinian Authority would weaken security cooperation, disrupt essential public services, marginalize pragmatic leadership in the West Bank, and create further openings for Hamas and other extremists.”

The letter is also signed by Reps. Gus Bilirakis (FL-12), Jimmy Panetta (CA-19), Ann Wagner (MO-02), and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (FL-25).

View the full text of the letter here and below.

Dear Secretary Bessent and Secretary Rubio:

We write to urge continued attention to preventing Hamas and other Iran-backed bad actors from exploiting economic instability in the West Bank. A fiscal crisis that weakens the Palestinian Authority creates exactly the kind of vacuum these groups seek to exploit for recruitment, weapons smuggling, and the erosion of security cooperation with Israel. A functioning economy in the West Bank is also important to establish greater stability for Palestinian citizens, fostering responsible and accountable governance, sustaining Israel’s long-term security, and preserving momentum toward broader regional integration, including continued expansion of the Abraham Accords.

We recognize Israel’s legitimate security concerns since October 7, and we are not asking for Israel to relax vigilance against terror financing. However, continued withholding of billions in clearance revenues risks accelerating the West Bank’s fiscal collapse – an outcome that would serve the interests of extremist and Iran-backed groups, not Israel, nor the United States. We therefore urge you to work with Israel and the Palestinian Authority on practical, security conscious mechanisms that keep clearance revenues flowing to legitimate Palestinian institutions while ensuring none are diverted to terror financing. All parties, including the Palestinian Authority, must do their part. Continued reform and anti-corruption measures by the Palestinian Authority are necessary to advance responsible fiscal treatment by the Israeli government. Paired together, these reforms and fiscal actions will support the greater regional stability we all seek.

The West Bank economy has historically been comparatively strong, with higher real GDP per capita than Jordan and a Human Development Index score in the high-human-development category. Notwithstanding serious economic problems, particularly in refugee camps, this relative prosperity has shown the value of moderation, secular government, and private enterprise. The contrast is especially stark when compared with Hamas’s authoritarian governance over Gaza before October 7, 2023, and the material deprivation of the civilians in Gaza since Hamas’s attack on Israel.

There can be no doubt that the success of the West Bank is due in part to high levels of human capital and deep integration with Israel’s economy. Additionally, the West Bank private sector depends on functioning correspondent banking relationships and the timely transfer of clearance revenues collected by Israel on behalf of the Palestinian Authority.

We are concerned that the Finance Ministry’s decision to hold clearance revenue transfers, combined with longstanding failures of governance and reform by the Palestinian Authority, is undermining these relationships and endangering the future of the West Bank. The Trump Administration has appropriately paired support for viable Palestinian institutions with clear demands for reform and accountability. The State Department welcomed the Palestinian Authority’s February 2025 decree restructuring its prisoner-payment system as an apparently positive step while making clear that serious concerns remain as to whether these reforms satisfy the Taylor Force Act, which Congress enacted to end the P.A.’s abhorrent pay for slay practice. We appreciate your commitment to ending this program and refusal to presume compliance before sufficient evidence has been presented. Secretary Rubio, your work through President Trump’s Board of Peace similarly reflects the Administration’s recognition that defeating Hamas requires credible, accountable Palestinian governance. And Secretary Bessent, under your leadership, Treasury has aggressively targeted Hamas’s illicit financial networks while distinguishing them from legitimate Palestinian interests.

We appreciate the efforts by your respective Departments to preserve correspondent banking relationships between Israeli and Palestinian banks. The State Department welcomed Israel’s extension of indemnification through the end of 2026 and correctly warned that destabilizing regulated banking channels, as we are presently seeing, would push transactions toward cash and other unregulated systems, undermining efforts to combat money laundering and terrorist financing.

We share the United States’ long-held position that the Palestinian Authority must implement meaningful reforms. Real and sustainable reform, however, cannot succeed if the Palestinian institutions expected to carry it out are deprived of the revenues and financial infrastructure necessary to function. Despite its significant shortcomings and flaws, the Palestinian Authority remains the only current viable governing alternative to Hamas and thus must play an essential role in promoting regional stability and security. A fiscal collapse of the Palestinian Authority would weaken security cooperation, disrupt essential public services, marginalize pragmatic leadership in the West Bank, and create further openings for Hamas and other extremists.

We ask you to continue your efforts to elevate accountability and ensure a viable future for the West Bank economy. With the risk of increased hostilities involving Iran continuing across the Middle East, we must prevent further instability in the region. We look forward to your response and request that you provide a classified briefing when Congress returns to Washington on the progress you have made on this issue over the summer.
title: SCHNEIDER, GOLDMAN LEAD BIPARTISAN EFFORT URGING SECRETARIES RUBIO AND BESSENT TO PREVENT FURTHER MIDDLE EASTERN INSTABILITY BY PROTECTING THE WEST BANK ECONOMY

Today, U.S. Representative Rick Larsen (WA-02) released the following statement:

“President Trump’s U.S. Postal Service (USPS) mail-in voting rule is an effort to suppress the right to vote. There is no evidence that mail-in ballots result in widespread voter fraud in our elections, no matter what the President claims.

“For instance, during a recount of ballots mailed in Whatcom County for last month’s primary, election workers confirmed that 100% of the ballots were counted accurately. Local election officials know how to administer free and fair elections.

“I am challenging Trump’s voter suppression efforts. I will keep supporting all efforts to defend Washington’s secure vote-by-mail system and protect the right of every eligible citizen to cast a ballot and have that ballot counted.”

Yesterday, Rep. Larsen joined 260 of his House and Senate colleagues in sending an amicus brief to the Supreme Court arguing against the legality of Trump’s USPS mail-in voting rule. The court case challenges a USPS rule issued because of President Trump’s executive order this past March that imposes unconstitutional and unworkable restrictions on mail-in voting, including requiring states to provide a “citizenship verification list” and attempting to give USPS control over who can vote by mail.

Rep. Larsen is a co-founder of the Congressional Voting Rights Caucus.

To read the full amicus brief, click here.
title: Larsen Pushes Back Against Trump’s Voter Suppression Efforts

JEFFERSON CITY, Mo. – A Columbia, Mo. man was sentenced in federal court today for possessing a firearm after a prior felony conviction.

Semaj Reshod Clark, 25, was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Stephen R. Bough to 120 months in prison, to be followed by three years of supervised release. Clark had previously pleaded guilty to one count of being a felon in possession of a firearm, admitting that he possessed a Taurus, model G3, 9 mm semi-automatic handgun in Boone County on Aug. 10, 2025.

According to government filings, Clark was found in possession of the firearm after an individual called law enforcement, reporting that Clark was at the individual’s home and was refusing to leave. When officers arrived, Clark fled on foot before being located and arrested with a loaded firearm in his pocket. Clark has prior felony convictions and was not permitted to possess a firearm.

This case is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney Lauren E. Kummerer. It was investigated by the Columbia Police Department and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives.
title: Columbia Man Sentenced to 10 Years for Firearm Offense

CISA Releases Updated Insider Threat Guide With New Insights to Mitigate Physical and Cyber Threats
WASHINGTON – The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) released today the updated Insider Threat Mitigation Guide which provides security support consistent with our statutory mission. The guide gives organizations a current look at insider threats and practical steps to develop or enhance an insider threat program. Delivered in a more streamlined format, the updated guide addresses evolving considerations such as the rise in hybrid and remote work, and advances in artificial intelligence (AI).
First published in 2020, the Insider Threat Mitigation Guide supports security and human resource professionals who manage insider threat programs, as well as leaders at every level of an organization. The guide was updated to acknowledge the growing impact insider threats have on critical infrastructure, the dynamic and evolving operational landscape, and provide new use cases to help organizations address new challenges. Any organization, regardless of the maturity level of its security, can leverage the guide to bolster their threat mitigation program.
“Insider threats continue to evolve as technology becomes more advanced. We urge organizations to establish a mitigation program that protects key assets, prevent violence, reduce losses, safeguard sensitive data, and save lives,” said Acting Executive Assistant Director for Infrastructure Security Scott Breor. “CISA appreciates the industry and government partner feedback that informed this timely update. CISA encourages organizations to review this updated guide, assess their program, and recommended steps to bolster their threat mitigation program.”
This updated guide gives employees an understanding of behavioral indicators that may signal a risk. Key updates in the guide include:
- New case studies, statistics, and section consolidation designed to enhance the original content, streamline information delivery, and ensure continued relevance.
- Expanded insights on emerging workplace trends such as increased hybrid and remote work, AI used to manipulate or deceive, and new content on access control, visitor screening, and mitigating the risk of adverse employee separations.
- Access to newly released CISA resources supporting preparedness and early risk detection.
For more information, please visit Insider Threat Mitigation Resources and Tools.
###
About CISA
As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.
Visit CISA.gov for more information and follow us on X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram.
title: CISA Releases Updated Insider Threat Guide With New Insights to Mitigate Physical and Cyber Threats

Washington, D.C. — Current and former Members of Congress mobilized in a court filing challenging the legality of President Donald Trump’s Executive Order seeking to exert control over mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The effort was led by House Administration Ranking Member Joe Morelle; Assistant House Minority Leader Joe Neguse, who leads the House Democrats’ Litigation Task Force; and Task Force Co-Chairs Oversight Ranking Member Robert Garcia and Judiciary Ranking Member Jamie Raskin. In the Senate, the brief was championed by Rules Committee Ranking Member Alex Padilla; Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer; Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin; and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee Ranking Member Gary Peters.

The group, made up of a bipartisan, bicameral coalition of 261 lawmakers, filed an amicus brief to the Supreme Court of the United States in the matter of United States Postal Service, et al., v. State of California, et al., a lawsuit brought by a coalition of State Attorneys General against the U.S. Postal Service. The court case challenges a Final Rule issued by the USPS pursuant to Trump’s directive that imposes unconstitutional and unworkable restrictions on mail-in voting, including requiring states to provide a “citizenship verification list” and attempting to give USPS control over who can vote by mail.

One-third of Americans are expected to vote by mail in the upcoming midterm elections—a voting practice Donald Trump himself used as recently as August 2026, when the president voted in Florida’s Republican primary.

In the court filing, the amici curiae argue that Trump’s Executive Order 14399, “Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections,” violates the separation of powers and usurps congressional authorities outlined in Article I of the U.S. Constitution, which gives the states and Congress exclusive authority over election administration.

“As current and former legislators, amici took an oath to uphold and defend the Constitution of the United States—including its guarantee of the separation of powers. Amici have a particular interest in defending the institutional role of the Legislative Branch under Article I of the Constitution and in vindicating the long-settled principle that the Constitution commits ultimate regulatory authority over federal elections to Congress. The Constitution does not contemplate the Executive Branch acting unilaterally to assert power over federal elections. Yet that is what the Order and Final Rule do,” wrote the lawmakers.

The amici also pointed to a recent federal court ruling blocking the USPS from implementing its newly finalized mail ballot rule for the midterm elections, saying the agency lacked the authority to implement the rule and that its actions are “substantively unconstitutional and contrary to law.”

“The district court correctly concluded that Appellees are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims that USPS lacked authority to issue the Final Rule, that the Final Rule unconstitutionally imposes mail-ballot requirements on the States, and that the Final Rule unconstitutionally bars non-compliant State and local election officials from using the USPS to mail ballots at all.”

The group concluded by asserting States’ power to administer elections and Congress’s power to make or alter rules regulating elections, which the Supreme Court itself has described as an “override” authority. The president’s illegal incursion on this authority is an attempt to disenfranchise people who depend on mail-in ballots to vote.

The lawmakers concluded: “The integrity of our constitutional system depends on each branch keeping to its assigned role. The Framers set up a two-part system that gave the States default authority to regulate federal elections subject to Congress’s authority to override the States. The Framers did not provide the President with any authority to interfere in that system, nor has Congress imbued the Executive Branch with any such authority by statute.”
title: Over 250 Current & Former Members of Congress Urge Supreme Court to Block Trump’s Executive Order Limiting Mail Voting

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Michigan Congresswoman Haley Stevens alongside Rep. Steven Horsford (NV-4) led their colleagues in calling on U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Commissioner Rodney Scott to immediately address administrative backlogs preventing American businesses from receiving refunds for duties paid under the Trump Administration’s illegal use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

Businesses have reported that delays in CBP’s Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (CAPE) system are preventing importers from meeting the agency’s 90-day deadline to request refunds — potentially costing small businesses money they are legally owed.

“Sadly, businesses in our districts have reported significant logistical hurdles that they must clear to receive a refund,” the lawmakers wrote. “Under no circumstances should these companies bear the brunt of both the tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court and the denial of tariff refunds because of administrative mismanagement of the CAPE system.”

“Michigan businesses should not have to pay the price once let alone twice, first through illegal tariffs, and again because government red tape prevents them from getting their money back,” said Rep. Haley Stevens. “Small businesses in Michigan operate on tight margins, and every dollar matters. CBP must fix these administrative roadblocks and make sure businesses receive every dollar they are owed.”

The Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that President Trump’s use of IEEPA to impose sweeping tariffs was unlawful. Rep. Stevens is urging CBP to take all necessary steps to ensure importers receive full refunds for duties paid under the invalidated tariff regime.

Full letter here.

###
title: Rep. Haley Stevens Demands Swift Refunds for Businesses Hit by Illegal Trump Tariffs

BROWNSVILLE, Texas – A 29-year-old woman has been sentenced for possession with intent to deliver cocaine.

Laura Janette Gonzalez pleaded guilty Sept. 21, 2025.

U.S. District Judge Rolando Olvera has now ordered Gonzalez to serve 25 months in federal prison to be immediately followed by two years of supervised release.

The investigation began in early 2024 when authorities identified Edgar Alejandro Villarreal, a/k/a Fresa, as a large-scale cocaine trafficker coordinating the smuggling, transportation, and distribution of multi-kilogram quantities of cocaine from Mexico into the United States.

During surveillance operations April 16, 2024, law enforcement observed Gonzalez and others arrive at a Weslaco parking lot in a Chevrolet Equinox to deliver narcotics. After spotting authorities, they fled.

Authorities conducted a traffic stop resulted in the discovery of a gift-wrapped box containing approximately 8.8 kilograms of cocaine.

The investigation revealed Villarreal and Edith Gonzalez, Laura Janette Gonzalez’s sister, coordinated the shipment that Laura Janette Gonzalez was to deliver.

Both Villarreal, 38, Brownsville, and Edith Gonzalez, 45, Donna, pleaded guilty. Edith Gonzalez received a 78-month-term, while Villarreal is scheduled to be sentenced Oct 21.

Laura Gonzalez has been and will remain in custody pending transfer to a Federal Bureau of Prisons facility to be determined in the near future.

This operation is part of the Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) initiative, established by Executive Order 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. The HSTF is a whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad. Through historic interagency collaboration, the HSTF directs the full might of U.S. law enforcement toward identifying, investigating, and prosecuting the full spectrum of crimes committed by these organizations, which have long fueled violence and instability within our borders. In performing this work, the HSTF places special emphasis on investigating and prosecuting those engaged in child trafficking or other crimes involving children. The HSTF further utilizes all available tools to prosecute and remove the most violent criminal aliens from the United States. HSTF South Texas/Houston comprises agents and officers from Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations; FBI; Drug Enforcement Administration; Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms, and Explosives; U.S. Marshals Service; U.S. Postal Inspection Service; Department of Transportation; IRS Criminal Investigation; Interpol/Department of State; and Naval Criminal Investigative Service with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Texas leading the prosecution.

Brownsville Police Department also assisted in this investigation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Oscar Ponce prosecuted the case.
title: Second cocaine trafficker receives prison sentence in Homeland Security Task Force investigation

United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jamie McDonald, announced today that NOSSON SKLAR, a/k/a “Nathan Sklar,” was sentenced to 38 months in prison for engaging in a scheme to defraud health benefit programs through the submission of more than $20 million in fraudulent claims.

“Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of this crime and our Office’s commitment to safeguarding affordable health care from fraud for all New Yorkers,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Nosson Sklar spent years bilking health care benefit programs of millions of dollars and will now spend serious time in prison for his conduct.”

“Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of this crime and our Office’s commitment to safeguarding affordable health care from fraud for all New Yorkers,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Nosson Sklar spent years bilking health care benefit programs of millions of dollars and will now spend serious time in prison for his conduct.”

According to the charging instruments, other public filings, and statements in public court proceedings:

SKLAR was the owner and chief executive officer of a company that operated a series of physical rehabilitation facilities around New York City (the “Rehabilitation Company”). Between at least January 2020 and in or about July 2024, SKLAR submitted or caused others to submit more than $20 million in claims for medical services to various health care benefit programs, asserting that those services were rendered by a physician who worked with the Rehabilitation Company (“Victim-1”). But that was false. Victim-1 did not provide those services, did not work with the Rehabilitation Company during that time, and did not authorize SKLAR to submit bills in his name.

In or about July 2024, Victim-1 spoke with SKLAR on at least two occasions about the fraudulent bills. During those conversations, SKLAR admitted that he had committed “fraud” by billing under Victim-1’s name, and that he did it “because [of] the money.”

Between at least in or about January 2020 and in or about July 2024, SKLAR caused more than $20 million in claims to be submitted to three separate health benefit programs (the “Health Plans”), which listed Victim-1 as having been the rendering provider for the Rehabilitation Company. Approximately $12.4 million of those claims were eventually paid by the Health Plans.

* * *

In addition to the prison term, SKLAR, 56, of New York, New York, was sentenced to three years of supervised release and ordered to forfeit $12,440,000 and to pay Victim-1’s legal expenses.

Mr. McDonald praised the outstanding investigative work of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General and Federal Bureau of Investigation.

This case is being handled by the Office’s White Plains Division. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jorja N. Knauer and David A. Markewitz are in charge of the prosecution.
title: Owner Of Physical Rehabilitation Company Sentenced To 38 Months In Prison For $20 Million Fraud On Health Benefit Programs

Trump’s Transportation Department Launches New SPACE Task Force to Unleash Commercial Space Innovation
The Trump Administration is moving to make space launches faster, more cost-effective, and keep the U.S. ahead
WASHINGTON, D.C. – U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy today launched the Space Policy Administration, Coordination, and Execution (SPACE) Task Force–an intradepartmental body that will coordinate space policy activities on behalf of the Department. The task force will implement the President’s National Space Transportation Policy that include recommendations to expand launch infrastructure, streamline regulation, better integrate the airspace, and coordinate space policy on behalf of USDOT.
“Under President Trump, the U.S. is leading in commercial space innovation. America had 217 of the 329 commercial space launches worldwide in 2025 and we expect that number to soar to 10,000 FAA-licensed launches and reentries yearly by 2035. This SPACE Task Force is going to ensure this next era of space transportation is led by America–not China,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy.
The Department’s SPACE Task Force will lead and coordinate a unified commercial space transportation strategy. It will focus on strengthening national security, bolstering our economic competitiveness, and unleashing innovation to secure America’s space dominance in the race against China.
“Keeping America’s edge in commercial space is key to advancing the economic and national security of the United States, and thanks to President Trump, USDOT is empowered like never before to advance this national priority,” said Under Secretary Ryan McCormack. “The SPACE Task Force will develop and coordinate space policy to achieve the aims of the National Space Transportation Policy and strengthen American leadership in this vital sector.”
Additional Information:
The SPACE Task Force–chaired by Under Secretary McCormack–brings together experts from the several DOT components, including: the Federal Aviation Administration, Office of General Counsel, Office of Research and Technology, Office of Transportation Policy, Office of Multimodal Freight Policy, and Office of Aviation and International Affairs.
In addition to announcing an initiative to develop new space launch routes, Secretary Duffy recently shared three key efforts to supercharge space port construction:
- An investment into commercial space facility roadways,
